title: See-through and opaque: how we see clear things, and what really stops light

summary.text: A clear glass marble is easy to see in the air, yet in a jar of honey it almost vanishes. Nothing about the marble changed. Your child tests clear things in water, oil and honey, and finds that we never see a clear thing itself, only what it does to light at its edges. Then two see-through filters laid together turn dark, a heap of clear sugar crystals looks white, and an X-ray sees through a hand that stops sunlight. Along the way, you find out why the sea loses its colours one by one, and how an animal can be see-through and still be seen.
summary.art: A clear glass marble clearly visible on a table beside a jar of honey in which an identical marble has almost vanished, leaving only a faint ring.

intro.hook: Put a clear glass marble in a jar of honey, and it almost vanishes. Take it out and it is easy to see again. The marble did not change, and neither did the honey. So what were you looking at when you saw the marble in the air?
intro.text: A window is see-through, but we are very good at noticing when there is one, because we see the frame, the dust and the glints on the glass. In this unit you find out why we can see clear things at all, and what happens to every bit of light that falls on something. You will make a clear thing vanish, turn clear crystals white, and make two see-through filters give darkness. You will also meet some waves that go straight through things that stop light completely.
intro.art: A hand lifting a clear glass marble out of a jar of honey, with the marble becoming visible again in the air above the jar.

outcomes: I can explain that we see a clear thing only where light bends or bounces at its edges, and use this to explain why a clear marble almost vanishes in honey.
I can say that every bit of light that meets a material is bounced back, soaked up, scattered or passed on, and that these shares add up to all of it.
I can explain that each layer of a see-through material lets through the same share of the light, so that light fades in steps such as a half, a quarter and an eighth.
I can explain why a heap of clear crystals, such as sugar, salt or snow, looks white.
I can explain why glass is clear, why a tiny trace of another material can colour a clear crystal, and why ordinary glass blocks most ultraviolet light.
I can use two polarising filters to show that light has a wiggle direction, and explain why two see-through filters can make darkness.
I can give examples of waves that go through things that are opaque to light, such as X-rays and radio waves.
I can run a fair test with a guess and a reason, and finish it like a scientist: what I think, what I saw, and why.

terms.meaning: A material that lets light pass straight through, so you can see clearly through it.
terms.example: A clean glass window and clear water are transparent.
terms.art: A clean glass window with a bright tree clearly visible through the glass.

terms.meaning: A material that lets light through, but scatters it, so you cannot see a clear picture through it.
terms.example: Butter paper and a frosted bathroom window are translucent. They glow, but show no clear view.
terms.art: A frosted bathroom window glowing white, with a blurry dark shape of a plant behind the glass.

terms.meaning: A material that does not let visible light through. Its surface bounces or soaks up all the light.
terms.example: A steel plate, a wooden door and a brick wall are opaque.
terms.art: A brick wall with a closed wooden door and no light coming through.

terms.meaning: When light goes through a material and out of the other side. Scientists also say that the light is transmitted.
terms.example: Most sunlight that falls on a clean window is passed on into the room.
terms.art: A beam of light going through a clean window pane into a room.

terms.meaning: To soak up. When a material absorbs light, the light's energy goes into the material and usually warms it a little.
terms.example: A black shirt in the Sun feels hot because it absorbs most of the light.
terms.art: A black shirt on a washing line in bright sunshine with heat shimmering above it.

terms.meaning: To send light in many different directions. Light that is scattered goes everywhere instead of in one straight path.
terms.example: Milk scatters light, so it looks white, and you cannot see through it.
terms.art: A beam of light hitting a glass of milk and spreading out in all directions.

terms.meaning: A number that tells how many times slower light moves in a material than in empty space. A bigger number means a bigger bend at the edge.
terms.example: Water is about 1.33, cooking oil about 1.47 and glass about 1.5.
terms.art: A row of blocks labelled water, oil and glass with a number printed on each.

terms.meaning: A liquid that bends light by almost the same amount as a clear solid in it. A clear thing placed in a matching liquid is very hard to see.
terms.example: A heat-proof glass rod nearly vanishes in cooking oil, because glass and oil bend light by almost the same amount.
terms.art: A glass rod in a jar of oil, fading to a faint outline halfway down.

terms.meaning: A solid whose tiny particles are lined up in a regular pattern. Crystals often have flat shiny faces.
terms.example: Rock sugar candy, rock salt and quartz are crystals.
terms.art: A lump of clear rock sugar candy with flat shiny faces on a plate.

terms.meaning: A tiny amount of a different material mixed into a pure material. A very small trace can change its colour.
terms.example: A trace of chromium turns clear aluminium oxide into a red ruby.
terms.art: A clear crystal on the left and a red ruby on the right, with a tiny dot of chromium shown between them.

terms.meaning: A tiny particle with an electric charge, found in every atom. Light can give an electron energy, and that is how materials soak up light.
terms.example: In a black cloth, electrons soak up the energy of visible light and the cloth warms.
terms.art: An atom drawn as a small centre with tiny dots circling it, and a ray of light hitting one dot.

terms.meaning: A repeating wiggle that carries energy from place to place. Light is a wave, and so are radio waves and X-rays.
terms.example: When you shake a skipping rope up and down, you send a wave along it.
terms.art: A skipping rope held by two children with a wave travelling along it.

terms.meaning: Light whose waves all wiggle in the same direction, for example only up and down. Ordinary sunlight wiggles in every direction at once.
terms.example: Light from many laptop and phone screens is polarised. So is the glare bouncing off a wet road.
terms.art: A rope passing through a narrow upright slot so that only up-and-down wiggles get through.

terms.meaning: A see-through sheet that lets through only light that wiggles in one direction. It works like a gate with upright bars.
terms.example: Polarising sunglasses cut the glare from water and wet roads.
terms.art: A pair of sunglasses with tiny parallel lines drawn on the lenses and two wiggling light waves, one going through and one blocked.

terms.meaning: An invisible kind of light with much more energy than visible light. X-rays go through soft body parts, but bones stop many of them.
terms.example: At a hospital, an X-ray picture shows the bones inside a hand.
terms.art: A hand held in front of a glowing X-ray plate, showing dark bones inside.

terms.meaning: A tiny, ghostly particle made in the Sun and in stars. Almost all neutrinos pass through the whole Earth without being stopped.
terms.example: About 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimetre of your skin each second, and you feel nothing.
terms.art: Thin lines streaming from the Sun through the Earth and out the other side, with a child standing on it.

terms.meaning: A material that darkens in strong light and clears again in the dark. Some spectacle lenses are photochromic.
terms.example: Photochromic spectacles go darker when you walk out into the Sun, and lighter again indoors.
terms.art: A pair of spectacles shown clear indoors on the left and dark in sunshine on the right.

terms.meaning: A part of a whole, written as a fraction or a percentage. We use shares to say how much of the light is bounced, soaked up, scattered or passed on.
terms.example: If a window passes on 9 out of every 10 parts of the light, the share that passes is nine tenths.
terms.art: A circle divided into ten equal slices with nine shaded yellow and one grey.

explanations.concept: Four things can happen to light: bounce, soak, scatter or pass on
explanations.definition: Every bit of light that falls on a material has one of four fates. It can bounce back, be soaked up, be scattered in many directions, or pass on through. The four shares always add up to the whole of the light that fell.
explanations.description: Think of 100 equal parts of light falling on a material. A clean window passes on about 90 of them. About 8 bounce back, a little from the front surface and a little from the back, and about 2 are soaked up by the glass. 90 plus 8 plus 2 makes 100. A mirror bounces back about 90 or more and soaks up the rest. Black velvet soaks up nearly all of it. A frosted window scatters most of the light that gets through, so you cannot see a clear picture through it. We call a material transparent when most light passes on in straight lines, translucent when light passes on but is scattered, and opaque when none passes on. These are not three separate kinds of stuff. They are three ways of sharing out the same light. No material is perfectly one thing. Even a clean window bounces some light back, which is why you can see a faint picture of the room in it at night.
examples: A clean glass window passes on about nine tenths of the light and bounces about one twelfth of it back.
A mirror bounces back most of the light, and soaks up the rest.
Black velvet soaks up nearly all the light that falls on it, so it looks very dark.
explanations.art: A circle of 100 small light dots falling on a window: 90 going through, 8 bouncing back and 2 shown fading inside the glass.
explanations.context: This card explains the four things that can happen to light when it meets any material, and how we use them to describe transparent, translucent and opaque things.

explanations.concept: Each layer takes the same share: fading in steps
explanations.definition: When light goes through several layers of the same material, each layer lets through the same share of the light that reaches it. So the light fades in steps, such as a half, then a quarter, then an eighth.
explanations.description: Suppose one sunglass lens lets half of the light through. Put a second identical lens behind it. The second lens does not take half of the original light. It takes half of what reached it. So the light after two lenses is half of a half, which is a quarter. After three lenses it is half of a quarter, which is an eighth. After four lenses it is a sixteenth. The light never quite reaches zero, but it soon becomes too faint to notice. If each layer passes nine tenths, as a clean window does, then two windows pass 81 parts out of 100, three pass about 73, and ten windows pass only about 35. This is why thick glass is darker at the edges, why the water at the bottom of a deep pool is dark, and why a thick stack of paper hides a lamp that a single sheet does not. The rule works for any material that soaks up light evenly through its depth. Scientists call it the Beer-Lambert law, after two scientists of the 1700s and 1800s.
examples: Four identical sunglass lenses held in a row let through only one sixteenth of the light.
Ten clean windows in a row let through only about a third of the light.
A thin slice of rock lets light through, and a thick piece of the same rock does not.
explanations.art: A row of four identical sunglass lenses with a bar chart above showing the light left after each one: a half, a quarter, an eighth and a sixteenth.
explanations.context: This card explains why light fades in steps as it goes through more layers, and how to work out how much is left.

explanations.concept: How we see a clear thing at all: the edges
explanations.definition: We see a clear thing only because light bends or bounces where its edges meet the air. If the thing is put in a liquid that bends light by the same amount, there is no bend at the edge, and the clear thing almost vanishes.
explanations.description: Look at a clear glass marble. The light that passes through its middle goes straight on, and your eye sees only what is behind. What you actually see is the edge, where light bends as it goes in and out, a little light bounces, and a few scratches and bubbles catch the light. The refractive index of glass is about 1.5. Air is about 1. That difference makes a strong bend at the edge, so the marble shows up clearly. Water is about 1.33, so the marble is a little less obvious in water. Cooking oil is about 1.47, and honey about 1.49 to 1.5, very close to glass. In honey, the light hardly bends at the edge, so there is almost nothing to see. A heat-proof glass rod nearly vanishes in cooking oil for the same reason. Water beads that children play with are about 99 parts water, so they nearly vanish in a glass of water. This is also why a wet piece of paper looks more see-through, and why wet cloth looks darker, because the water fills the gaps between the fibres and bends light less. A clear thing is not invisible. It is only invisible where it does not change the light.
examples: A clear glass marble nearly vanishes in a jar of honey.
A heat-proof glass rod almost disappears in a jar of cooking oil.
Jelly-like water beads nearly vanish in a glass of water.
explanations.art: Three jars side by side containing the same clear marble: in air it is bright and sharp, in water a little fainter, and in honey only a faint ring remains.
explanations.context: This card explains how we see clear things, and why a clear thing seems to vanish when it is put in a liquid that bends light by the same amount.

explanations.concept: Why a heap of clear crystals looks white
explanations.definition: A heap of clear crystals looks white because light bends and bounces off the many small surfaces of the crystals, over and over. It comes back out of the heap in all directions, mixed together, and mixed light looks white.
explanations.description: Rock sugar candy, called kalkandu or mishri, is clear. Grind it to powder and it turns white. Each tiny grain is still clear, but now there are thousands of grains, each with many surfaces. Light enters a grain, bends, bounces off the next surface, and goes into another grain. It zigzags through the heap and soon comes back out in a random direction. Little of it gets through, and none goes straight. All the colours of light get scattered about the same, so the heap looks white. The same happens with salt, with snow, with the foam on a glass of lassi, with clouds and with fog. Snow is made of clear ice crystals. Clouds are made of clear water droplets. Milk is white because its tiny drops of fat and clumps of protein scatter light. If you put a drop of oil on the sugar powder, the oil fills the gaps between the grains. The light then bends less, and the patch looks darker and more see-through. White paint is mostly clear plastic with a powder of a very white mineral, which scatters light strongly.
examples: Rock sugar candy is clear, and the same sugar ground to powder is white.
Snow is made of clear ice crystals, yet snow looks white.
Wet cloth looks darker than dry cloth, because water between the fibres makes them scatter less.
explanations.art: A lump of clear rock sugar candy next to a heap of white sugar powder, with a zigzag ray of light bouncing through the grains and coming out of the heap in many directions.
explanations.context: This card explains why clear sugar, salt, snow and ice turn white when they are broken into small pieces, and why oil makes them see-through again.

explanations.concept: Why glass is clear and a ruby is red: electrons and energy
explanations.definition: A material soaks up a colour of light only if the light's energy matches a jump that its electrons can make. In glass, the smallest jump is bigger than the energy of visible light, so visible light passes on. Ultraviolet light has more energy, and glass soaks it up.
explanations.description: Everything is made of atoms, and atoms have electrons. An electron can take energy from light, but only in a jump of one particular size. Light comes in tiny packets of energy called photons. A photon of red light carries less energy than a photon of violet, and a photon of ultraviolet carries even more. In glass, the electrons are held tightly. The smallest jump they can make needs more energy than any photon of visible light carries. So visible light cannot be soaked up, and it passes on. That is why glass is clear. Ultraviolet photons are strong enough for the jump, so ordinary window glass soaks up most of the ultraviolet B that causes sunburn. In a metal, some electrons are free to move, and they soak up and bounce back all visible light, so metals are opaque and shiny. Pure aluminium oxide is clear. A trace of chromium turns it into a red ruby. A trace of iron and titanium turns it into a blue sapphire. Thick window glass looks green at its edge because of a trace of iron in it. A tiny impurity can make a clear crystal red, because it adds a jump of just the right size to soak up one colour.
examples: Ordinary window glass passes visible light, but blocks most of the ultraviolet B that burns the skin.
A ruby and a sapphire are both aluminium oxide, a clear crystal with different traces of other materials.
The edge of a thick sheet of window glass looks green because of a trace of iron.
explanations.art: A zoom into glass with an atom, an electron on a low step, and arrows for red, blue and ultraviolet light, where only the long ultraviolet arrow is tall enough to lift the electron up.
explanations.context: This card goes down to the atoms to explain why glass lets visible light through, and why a trace of another material can colour a clear crystal.

explanations.concept: Two see-through filters can make darkness: polarised light
explanations.definition: Light is a wave that wiggles across the direction it travels. A polarising filter lets through only light that wiggles in one direction. Two filters turned at right angles to each other block almost all the light, though each one is see-through on its own.
explanations.description: Imagine a skipping rope tied to a post, running through a fence with upright bars. If you shake the rope up and down, the wiggle goes through the gap. If you shake it side to side, the bars stop it. A polarising filter is like that fence for light. It has tiny stretched chains of molecules, all lined up in one direction. Ordinary light from the Sun or a bulb wiggles in every direction, so a filter lets through about half of it, in one direction only, and you simply see a darker world. If you add a second filter turned a quarter of a turn, the light that got through the first wiggles up and down, and the second filter only passes side-to-side wiggles. Almost nothing gets through. The two see-through filters give darkness. Turn the second filter slowly and the light comes back, brightest when the filters line up. Light from the screen of a laptop or phone is already polarised, so one filter is enough to make it go dark at one angle. If you place a third filter between two crossed ones, turned halfway, some light comes back. Scientists call this a surprising but well understood result.
examples: Two pairs of polarising sunglasses, with one pair turned a quarter turn, give almost complete darkness.
A phone screen seen through polarising sunglasses goes dark when you turn the glasses on their side.
Clear sticky tape between two crossed filters shows bands of colour.
explanations.art: A skipping rope with up-and-down waves passing through a fence of upright bars, and sideways waves stopped by the same fence, beside two crossed polarising sunglass lenses showing darkness where they overlap.
explanations.context: This card explains how two filters that are each see-through can block all light when they are put together the right way.

explanations.concept: Polarised light all around us: glare, screens and animals that use it
explanations.definition: Light that bounces off water, wet roads and glass is partly polarised. Polarising sunglasses cut that glare. Many animals, such as bees, ants and dung beetles, use the pattern of polarised light in the sky to find their way.
explanations.description: When sunlight bounces off a flat shiny surface, such as a pond or a wet road, the light that comes back wiggles mostly sideways, along the surface. Polarising sunglasses have their filters turned to block sideways wiggles, so they cut the glare and let you see into the water. This is why anglers and drivers like them. Sunlight is also partly polarised by the air in the sky, in a pattern that depends on where the Sun is. Bees and some desert ants can see this pattern and use it as a compass, even when the Sun is hidden behind a cloud. In 2003, Marie Dacke, a Swedish scientist, showed that dung beetles can roll their balls of dung in a straight line by the polarised light of the Moon. Cuttlefish and mantis shrimps are also reported to see polarised light. Human eyes mostly do not notice it. We know it is there only because we can build filters that show it.
examples: Polarising sunglasses make it easier to see fish through the glare on a pond.
Bees and desert ants use the polarised light of the sky as a compass.
Dung beetles can keep a straight line by the polarised light of the Moon.
explanations.art: A dung beetle rolling a ball of dung at night, with a faint pattern of polarised light across the Moonlit sky above and a straight path behind.
explanations.context: This card is about polarised light in everyday life and in nature, including the animals that see what we cannot.

explanations.concept: Opaque to light, but see-through to other waves: X-rays, radio and neutrinos
explanations.definition: Whether something is opaque depends on the kind of wave. A hand that stops visible light lets X-rays through. A brick wall that stops light lets many radio waves through. Neutrinos go through the whole Earth.
explanations.description: Light is one kind of wave. X-rays, radio waves and microwaves are others, with different amounts of energy. A material soaks up or lets through each kind in its own way. Skin and muscle let most X-rays pass, but bones soak up many of them. That is why a hospital X-ray shows bones as shadows. Radio waves from a mobile tower and Wi-Fi from a router pass through walls, though they get weaker, but they cannot pass through thick metal. Neutrinos are tiny particles made in the Sun's core. They pass through the Earth almost as if it were not there. About 60 billion of them go through every square centimetre of your skin every second, and almost none stop. To catch a few, scientists build huge detectors deep underground. So the words transparent and opaque only describe how a material treats one kind of wave. A wall that is opaque to light is nearly transparent to a neutrino. And glass, which is transparent to light, blocks most ultraviolet.
examples: A hospital X-ray shows the bones inside a hand that sunlight cannot pass.
Wi-Fi reaches the next room through a brick wall, though more weakly.
More than a hundred billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through your thumbnail every second.
explanations.art: A hand shown three ways: in sunlight as an opaque shadow, in X-rays as a ghostly image of bones, and with a stream of tiny neutrino dots passing right through the whole hand and the floor.
explanations.context: This card explains that opaque only means opaque to one kind of wave, and gives examples of waves that go through things that stop light.

explanations.concept: Glass that changes: darkening spectacles, switching windows and see-through wood
explanations.definition: Some clear materials can change how much light they pass on. Photochromic lenses darken in strong light. Switchable windows change with a small electric voltage. Scientists have also made wood that is partly see-through by removing its dark colour and filling its pores with clear plastic.
explanations.description: Photochromic spectacle lenses contain tiny crystals, or special molecules, that change when ultraviolet light from the Sun hits them. They then soak up more visible light, and the lenses turn dark. Out of the Sun, the change reverses, and the lenses clear again. Some office windows use a thin layer of liquid crystals. With the voltage off they scatter light and look frosted. With the voltage on the crystals line up and the glass turns clear. Some aeroplane windows, such as those on the Boeing 787, darken at the press of a button, through a different kind of coating. Scientists in Sweden and the USA have also made see-through wood, in the 2010s. They remove the dark colour of lignin from thin sheets of wood. Then they fill the tiny gaps with a clear plastic that bends light nearly the same as the wood fibres. That matches the refractive indexes, just as honey does for a marble. The result lets light through, and may one day be used for windows.
examples: Photochromic spectacle lenses darken outdoors in the Sun and clear indoors.
Switchable privacy glass is frosted when the power is off and clear when it is on.
Transparent wood is made by removing the dark colour and filling the gaps with matching clear plastic.
explanations.art: Three panels: spectacles that are clear indoors and dark outdoors, a frosted office window turning clear when a switch is flicked, and a thin slice of pale wood glowing as light passes through it.
explanations.context: This card is about materials that can switch between clear and dark, or clear and frosted, and about wood that scientists made see-through.

explanations.concept: The sea eats light colour by colour
explanations.definition: Clear water soaks up the different colours of light by different amounts. It soaks up red first, then orange, yellow and green, and lets blue through the furthest. So the deeper you go, the bluer the light, until it is all gone.
explanations.description: Water looks clear, but it is not perfectly transparent. A thick layer of it soaks up light, and it soaks up red much more than blue. Within about ten metres of the surface, most of the red light has been soaked up. A red object in water at that depth looks dark brown or black. By about 100 metres, only blue is left. The sunlit part of the ocean reaches down to about 200 metres. Below it, down to about 1,000 metres, is the twilight zone, where only a faint blue glow remains. Below 1,000 metres, no sunlight reaches at all, and the deep sea is dark except for light made by living beings. Many deep-sea animals are red. In blue light, a red animal looks black, so she is hard to see. Many animals of the open sea are also nearly see-through, such as jellyfish, comb jellies and the young stages of eels and shrimps. For them, being clear is a way to hide in water, which has a refractive index close to their own bodies.
examples: A red fish near the surface looks red. Deeper down, without a lamp, the same fish looks black.
Sunlight reaches about 200 metres into clear sea water.
Jellyfish are almost see-through because their bodies are mostly water.
explanations.art: A cross-section of the sea from the surface to deep water with the colour of the light changing from white to blue to black, and small red and clear animals at different depths.
explanations.context: This card explains why the sea gets bluer and then darker with depth, and why many sea animals are clear or red.

explanations.concept: How a see-through animal still gets seen
explanations.definition: Even the clearest animal has parts that stop light, so she can still be seen. Her eyes need dark pigment to catch light, her gut and bones scatter or soak it up, and her body casts a faint shadow. To see anything, an eye must stop some of the light that falls on it.
explanations.description: Think about what your own eye does. Light falls on the retina, and special cells soak up the light and send a signal to the brain. If the cells did not soak up any light, the light would pass through and there would be nothing to sense. So a perfectly see-through eye would see nothing. That is why almost every see-through animal still has dark eyes. The Indian glassy fish, a small freshwater fish found in ponds and slow rivers across India, is almost clear. Yet you can see her backbone as a thin silvery line, her two eyes as dark dots and her gut as a darker shape. Her body also bends and holds back a little light, so in bright sun she casts a faint, flickering shadow on the pond floor. Glass frogs of Central and South America are partly clear. A team reported in 2022 that they hide most of their red blood cells in their livers while they sleep. Being see-through gives only some hiding. A being has to be able to take in light to see, and to be made of cells that hold some light back. Hiding and seeing pull against each other.
examples: A clear glass-like fish shows two dark eye dots and a silvery backbone, but the rest of the body is almost invisible.
In bright sunlight, a clear fish casts a faint shadow on the sandy floor of a pond.
A jellyfish looks almost invisible, until a light shines from the side and shows the edges of her bell.
explanations.art: A tiny nearly clear fish in a pond with two dark dots for eyes, a thin silvery line along the back, and a faint, flicking shadow on the sand below her.
explanations.context: This card is about animals that are almost see-through, and why they are still not completely invisible.

explanations.description: People have used natural glass, such as volcanic obsidian, for tens of thousands of years. But the first made glass, melted and shaped by people, is harder to trace. Archaeologists agree that glass beads and glass vessels were being made in West Asia and Egypt by about 3,500 years ago. They do not agree on where the very first glass was made, or on how soon glass-making started elsewhere, including in India.
examples: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder told a story of sailors who made glass by accident on a beach, but most historians doubt it.
Glass beads and small objects have been found at ancient sites in India, and archaeologists argue about how old the earliest ones are.
Arikamedu, near Puducherry, was a trading town about 2,000 years ago where beads were made, including glass beads.

perspectives.who: Pliny the Elder, a Roman writer, about 77 CE
perspectives.explanation: In his book Natural History, he told the tale of sailors resting their cooking pots on blocks of natron on a beach. The heat, he said, melted the sand and the natron into glass. Modern experiments suggest that an ordinary campfire is not hot enough.

perspectives.who: Archaeologists of West Asia and Egypt
perspectives.explanation: The oldest glass vessels and many glass beads come from Mesopotamia and Egypt, from about 3,500 years ago. Many think glass-making began there, but earlier traces may be lost.

Glass beads have been found at sites in India that are thousands of years old. Some scholars think that glass-making in India started early and independently. Others think the ideas arrived from elsewhere. The dating of the early finds is still argued about.

explanations.art: Three small scenes in a row: sailors resting pots on blocks on a beach, a workshop in Egypt with a glass vessel being shaped, and a bead-maker at Arikamedu with a bowl of glass beads.
explanations.context: This card is about the argument over who first made glass, a clear material, and where.

agreed.text: Every bit of light that meets a material is bounced back, soaked up, scattered or passed on, and the four shares add up to all of it.
agreed.evidence: Instruments that measure light can measure how much is reflected, scattered and passed on. The part that is soaked up appears as a small rise in temperature. The shares always add up to the light that fell.

agreed.text: A clear thing nearly vanishes when it is placed in a clear liquid that bends light by almost the same amount.
agreed.evidence: A heat-proof glass rod nearly vanishes in cooking oil, and a glass marble nearly vanishes in honey. Scientists who study cells under a microscope use a special oil on purpose to match the glass of the lens.

agreed.text: A heap of clear crystals looks white because of scattering, and it turns clearer when its gaps are filled with a liquid that bends light the same.
agreed.evidence: Rock sugar candy is clear, and ground to powder it is white. A drop of oil on the powder makes the patch darker and more see-through.

agreed.text: Two polarising filters turned at right angles block almost all light, though each one on its own is see-through.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see this with two pairs of polarising sunglasses. The effect was described by the French physicist Étienne-Louis Malus in 1809.

agreed.text: Things that stop visible light can be see-through to other waves, such as X-rays and radio waves.
agreed.evidence: Hospital X-rays show bones through the skin. Mobile phone signals reach rooms with no window. Neutrino detectors catch particles that have come right through the Earth.

agreed.text: Ordinary glass passes visible light but blocks most ultraviolet B light.
agreed.evidence: Measurements with a spectrometer show this. It is why you are less likely to get a sunburn sitting behind a closed window.

challenging.claim: A clean window lets all of the light through.
challenging.who: Many people, because a clean window seems to be not there at all.
challenging.for: At noon you can see the garden perfectly, with all its colours.
challenging.against: A clean window bounces back about 8 parts in every 100 and soaks up a little more. At night with the light on, you can see yourself in it. About 90 parts in 100 pass on.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that clear glass lets all the light through.

challenging.claim: Anything that stops light stops every kind of ray.
challenging.for: Thick black cardboard stops all light, so it seemed natural that it would stop everything that behaves like light.
challenging.against: In 1895, Wilhelm Röntgen found rays that passed through black cardboard. X-rays go through skin, and radio waves go through walls.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that opaque things stop every kind of wave.

challenging.claim: A white powder must be made of a white material.
challenging.who: Many young children, and many grown-ups too.
challenging.for: Sugar powder, salt, flour and chalk all look white.
challenging.against: Sugar candy is clear. Salt crystals are clear. Even snow is made of clear ice. A heap of clear pieces scatters light in every direction, and so it looks white.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that things look white because they are made of something white.

challenging.claim: The darker the sunglasses, the better they protect your eyes.
challenging.who: A common belief when buying sunglasses.
challenging.for: Dark lenses cut a lot of bright light, which feels more comfortable.
challenging.against: Dark lenses with no ultraviolet filter let your pupils open wider, so more ultraviolet light can get into your eyes. Protection depends on the filter, not on the darkness. Look for a label that says that the lenses block ultraviolet.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea that darker sunglasses are safer.

challenging.claim: Glass was discovered by accident when sailors cooked on a beach.
challenging.who: The Roman writer Pliny the Elder, in about 77 CE, told this story.
challenging.for: Sand is the main ingredient of glass, and the story is simple and easy to remember.
challenging.against: A wood fire on a beach is not hot enough to melt sand, even with natron. Archaeologists find that early glass-makers used big furnaces and a lot of careful work.
challenging.context: This card is about an old story of how glass was invented.

challenging.claim: A see-through animal is completely invisible.
challenging.who: A common idea about glass frogs, jellyfish and glassy fish.
challenging.for: From a distance, many of them are very hard to spot.
challenging.against: Their eyes must be dark to see. Their gut and bones show, their edges bend light, and they cast faint shadows. Look with a light from the side, or against a dark background, and they appear.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that see-through animals cannot be seen.

big_questions.q: We see a glass marble only by what it does to light at its edge. Do we ever see a thing itself, or only what the thing does to light?
big_questions.hint: Think of the marble in honey. Is it still there when you cannot see it?

big_questions.q: An eye has to stop some light in order to see. What would a perfectly see-through eye see?
big_questions.hint: Think about what happens to light that goes straight through without being caught.

big_questions.q: Two see-through filters together are dark. What does this tell you about the words see-through and opaque?
big_questions.hint: See-through for which light? From which angle?

big_questions.q: A wall that stops light lets some radio waves through, and the Earth lets neutrinos through. Is anything really solid?
big_questions.hint: Solid for light, solid for a hand, and solid for a neutrino are not the same.

big_questions.q: Whose windows are see-through from one side only, and who decides who can see in and out?
big_questions.hint: Think of a jaali, a curtain, tinted car glass and a one-way mirror. Who sees, and who is seen?

big_questions.q: Being see-through helps animals hide in the sea, but a see-through eye cannot see. Is hiding always paid for with something else?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the glassy fish gave up to be almost clear.

big_questions.q: The hand that you see in the Sun, and the hand that an X-ray shows, are the same hand. Which one is the real hand?
big_questions.hint: Each kind of wave meets a different part of the hand.

big_questions.q: If every creature senses a different set of waves, what would the world look like to a being that could see X-rays and radio waves too?
big_questions.hint: Think of a bee seeing ultraviolet, a dung beetle seeing polarised moonlight, and a hospital machine seeing bones.

story.title: The Fish Nobody Could See
story.note: The Indian glassy fish is a real small fish that lives in ponds, canals and slow rivers across India. Her body is almost see-through, but her eyes, backbone and gut can be seen. The village, the pond, Revathi, her mother, her teacher Anitha Miss, the officer and everything that happens in the story are made up. A clear glass rod really does almost vanish in cooking oil if it is made of heat-proof glass.
text: Our village pond is called the Ambal Kulam. It lies behind the temple, with stone steps on all four sides, and a banyan tree leaning over the water like an old woman looking at her own face.

That summer, everyone said the pond was dead. The rains had failed twice. The water had gone low and green, and the panchayat had decided to fill the pond with earth and build a bus stand on top. 'A pond with no fish is a pond for nobody,' they said.

A man came from the district office to check. He wore a green shirt and carried a clipboard and a big net with wide holes. His name was Raghavan Sir. He swept the net through the water from three sides, slowly and carefully. Each time, he lifted it out and shook it. There was weed in it, and one wet plastic bag. Nothing else.
'No fish,' he said, quite kindly, and wrote those words on his clipboard. 'Dead pond.'

I am ten years old, and I have sat on those steps every evening of my life. I knew he was wrong. But what bothered me was that my own eyes agreed with him. When I leaned over the water, I saw green water, the stone steps and my own face. I saw no fish at all.

At school the next morning, Anitha Miss was showing us a trick. She stood a glass rod in a beaker of cooking oil. The rod vanished. 'Where has it gone?' she asked. Nobody knew. She lifted it out, and there it was. She put it back, and it was gone again.

'We do not really see clear things,' she said. 'We see what they do to light. Where a clear thing bends the light, or bounces some of it, or holds a little back, we see that. In oil, the glass bends light just like the oil does, so there is nothing to see.'

I thought about that all the way home. At noon I walked down the temple steps and crouched at the edge of the pond. The Sun was straight overhead. And on the sandy floor of the shallow end, I saw something move.

It was a shadow. A small, thin, flickering shadow, no bigger than my finger. Then there was another, and another. Dozens of them darted left together, turned, and came back, like a flock of birds crossing a field. But above the shadows, in the water, there was nothing. Not a flash, not a gleam. I rubbed my eyes. The shadows were still there.
'Shadows of what?' I said out loud.

Then I understood. What would a fish do to light, if she were made almost of water, and clear as glass? She would not bend it much. She would not bounce it much. But she would hold a little of it back. She would cast a faint shadow. And her eyes? An eye has to catch light to see. So her eyes must be dark. And her gut must be darker than the rest of her.

I ran home and fetched Amma's black cloth, and the steel tumbler from the kitchen. I came back and dipped the tumbler into the shallow end. I held it up in front of the black cloth, in the sunlight. And there they were.

Tiny fish, no longer than my thumb, with bodies like slivers of glass. Each one had two black dots for eyes, a thread of silver for a backbone, and a dark smudge for a gut. Everything else about her was nearly clear. I counted nine in my tumbler alone.
I took the tumbler and the cloth to the panchayat office. Raghavan Sir was drinking tea. 'Sir,' I said, 'please do not look for fish. Look for shadows.'

He frowned. But he came with me, in his green shirt, down the temple steps. I showed him the shadows on the sand, flicking and turning. I held the black cloth behind the tumbler and put it in his hands.
He looked for a long time. 'Your net,' I said, 'has very wide holes. And the fish are as clear as the water. How could you see them?'
He said nothing for a moment. Then he took out his pen, crossed out the two words on his clipboard, and counted. 'Hundreds,' he said at last. 'There are hundreds of them.'

The bus stand was built beside the school instead. And every evening I still sit on the steps of the Ambal Kulam. At noon, if the Sun is high, the shadows come, flicking across the sand like a flock of birds that nobody can see.
story.epiphany: For the parent: we do not see clear things themselves. We see the places where they change the light, by bending it, bouncing some, or holding some back. A glass rod vanishes in oil, because glass and oil bend light by almost the same amount. A nearly see-through fish still has dark eyes, a gut and a backbone, and she casts a faint shadow on the pond floor. The girl finds the fish by looking for what they do to light, instead of for the fish. An eye that let all the light through could not see, so even the clearest animal needs dark eyes.
ask: Why does a glass rod almost vanish when it is put into a jar of cooking oil, but not when it is in the air?
If an animal is nearly see-through, which parts of her body do you think can still be seen, and why?
Why must an eye stop some of the light that falls on it in order to see?
How could you find a see-through thing in a jar of water without touching it?
A net with wide holes catches only what is big enough. What else do we miss because of the tools we use to look?

how_we_found_out.story: In 1895, most scientists believed that a thick black cover stops all rays, just as it stops light. Wilhelm Röntgen, a German physicist in Würzburg, was working in a darkened room with a glass tube that gave off invisible rays. He had wrapped the tube in black cardboard, to be sure no light escaped. Yet a screen painted with a chemical, lying across the room, began to glow. Something was passing through the cardboard. He tried paper, wood and a thick book, and the screen still glowed. When he held his hand in front of the screen, he saw the dark shadows of his bones. In December 1895 he made a picture of the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, with her ring showing on one finger. He called the new rays X-rays, with X for unknown. In 1901 he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.
how_we_found_out.who: Wilhelm Röntgen, with the first X-ray picture of the hand of Anna Bertha Röntgen
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Scientists believed that anything opaque to light stops every kind of ray. Röntgen showed that rays can pass through black cardboard, wood and flesh, and that bones stop them, so opaque only describes how a material treats one kind of wave.

roots.context: We made a clear marble vanish, turned clear crystals white, and made see-through filters dark. Now we ask what this tells us about seeing, and about what is really there.

deep_truth.truth: We never see a clear thing itself. We see only the places where it bends, bounces or holds back light. In honey, which bends light just as glass does, a clear marble almost vanished. So seeing a clear thing is seeing what it does to light.
deep_truth.habit: We say that we see the things around us directly, just as they are. For clear things, what we see is only the place where light changes.
deep_truth.evidence: In the vanishing-glass test, the same marble was easy to see in air, harder in water and oil, and almost gone in honey. Only the liquid around it changed. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your eye has to stop some light in order to see it. The dark pigment at the back of the eye catches the light. A perfectly see-through eye could not see anything.
three.what_is_life: Many animals in the sea are almost clear, and yet they have dark eyes, and their shadows give them away. Hiding well and seeing well pull against each other.
three.what_is_this_world: Clear glass, white sugar, dark cloth and a see-through hand under X-rays are all the same matter meeting light in different ways. What a thing looks like depends on what meets it.

roots.thread: Clear, white and black are not three kinds of stuff. Each is a different way of sharing out the same light among bouncing, soaking, scattering and passing on. A pile of clear crystals is white, and a piece of clear glass in oil is gone. A hand that is opaque to sunlight is nearly clear to X-rays. So the world we see is a meeting between light and things, and not the things alone. What looks like many separate kinds of material is the same light meeting the world in different ways.

teachings.teaching: Thirty spokes meet at the hub of a wheel, but the empty space in the hub is what makes the wheel work. Clay is shaped into a pot, but the emptiness inside is what makes the pot useful. We cut doors and windows for a room, and it is the empty places that make the room useful.
teachings.link: A window is useful because it is the part that does not stop the light. The part of the world that we do not see is often what does the work.

teachings.source: Plato, Republic, Book 7 (the allegory of the cave)
teachings.teaching: Prisoners chained in a cave see only the shadows of objects on a wall, and they take the shadows for the real things. When one is freed and sees the objects, and then the Sun, he finds that the shadows were only part of the truth.
teachings.link: The girl found the fish by their shadows, but the shadows were not the fish. Seeing a shadow tells you something is there, and looking more closely tells you more.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son Shvetaketu to break open a banyan seed, and then break open one of the tiny seeds inside it. He sees nothing. His father says that the fine thing that he cannot see is the very thing from which the great tree grows.
teachings.link: What cannot be seen, such as a clear fish in water, can still be real. A being can be there even when nothing about her is visible.

science.text: No material is perfectly transparent. Even the clearest glass bounces some light and soaks up some, and every material is opaque to some kinds of wave.
How animals that see polarised light use it, and what it looks like to them, is still being studied.

other_view.view: The marble does not vanish in honey. It is still there, with the same weight and shape, and you could find it with your fingers. We only fail to see it. What we see is not the whole of what is there.

practice.title: Find the clear things
practice.say: Sit quietly and look around the room. Find three clear things, such as a window, a glass or a plastic bottle. For each one, find the place where you can see it. Is it the edge, a glint, a bubble or a reflection? Breathe in slowly three times. Then ask yourself what is clear in the room that you have not yet noticed.
practice.kid: Look around the room. Find three clear things. Find the place where you can see each one. Breathe slowly three times.

ask: If you cannot see a thing, is it still there? How could you find out?
A glass marble is gone in honey. Is it the marble that changed, or the way you see it?
If the eye must stop light to see, what else must be given up in order to know something?

games.title: Where Did the Light Go? Bounce, Soak, Scatter or Pass
games.players: 1 to 5 players. Alone, with a parent, or with friends.
games.context: This is a card game about the four things that can happen to light. For each card, players decide what happens to most of the light, and say why.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: light meeting something on the front, and where most of it goes on the back

items.f: PRACTICE CARD. Sunlight falls on a clean glass window.
items.b: PASSES ON. About nine tenths of the light goes through. About one twelfth bounces back, which is why you can see a faint picture of the room in a window at night.

items.f: Sunlight falls on a bathroom mirror.
items.b: BOUNCES. A mirror sends back most of the light in one tidy direction, so you see a picture of yourself.

items.f: Light falls on a piece of black velvet.
items.b: SOAKED UP. Black velvet takes in nearly all the light, and its energy warms the cloth a little.

items.f: A torch shines through a sheet of butter paper.
items.b: SCATTERED. Some light gets through, but it goes in every direction, so the paper glows and you cannot see a clear picture through it.

items.f: Sunlight falls on a heap of white sugar powder.
items.b: SCATTERED. It zigzags through the many tiny clear crystals and comes back out in all directions. That is why the heap looks white.

items.f: Light crosses from honey into a clear glass marble sitting in the honey.
items.b: PASSES ON. Honey and glass bend light by almost the same amount, so there is hardly any bounce or bend at the edge, and the marble almost vanishes.

items.f: Sunlight falls on fresh snow.
items.b: SCATTERED. Snow is made of clear ice crystals. Light bounces about among them and comes back out in all directions, so snow looks white.

items.f: Light falls on a thick sheet of black rubber.
items.b: SOAKED UP. Nearly all of it is taken in, and none passes through.

items.f: Sunlight goes through the fog on a winter morning in a hill town.
items.b: SCATTERED. Tiny drops of water bounce light in all directions, so you see a white glow and not far into the distance.

items.f: Sunlight goes down through 10 centimetres of clear water in a tumbler.
items.b: PASSES ON. A thin layer of clear water soaks up almost nothing.

items.f: Red light from the Sun goes down through 20 metres of sea water.
items.b: SOAKED UP. Water soaks up red light much more than blue, and most of the red is gone within about 10 metres.

items.f: Blue light from the Sun goes down through 20 metres of sea water.
items.b: PASSES ON. Water soaks up blue light much less than red, which is why the sea looks blue and why the deep light is blue.

items.f: Light falls on milk in a glass.
items.b: SCATTERED. Tiny drops of fat and clumps of protein bounce the light in all directions. Milk looks white, and you cannot see through it.

items.f: Sunlight falls on a dark sunglass lens.
items.b: SOAKED UP. A dark lens takes in more than half of the light and lets the rest through.

items.f: Red light falls on a green leaf.
items.b: SOAKED UP. A green leaf soaks up red light and uses its energy to make food. It sends back much of the green light, which is why it looks green.

items.f: Sunlight falls on a white-painted wall.
items.b: SCATTERED. The paint's tiny white grains bounce light in all directions, so the wall looks white from every side of the room.

items.f: Light reaches a pane of frosted glass in a bathroom window.
items.b: SCATTERED. The rough surface bends light in many directions. Light gets through, but you see no clear view.

items.f: X-rays fall on a hand.
items.b: PASSES ON. Most X-rays go through skin and muscle. Bones soak up many of them, which is why they show as shadows.

items.f: Wi-Fi radio waves meet a brick wall.
items.b: PASSES ON. Much of the signal goes through, but weaker. A thick metal sheet would bounce or soak it up.

items.f: Sunlight, low in the evening sky, falls on a calm pond.
items.b: BOUNCES. At a very low angle, the water's surface works like a mirror and sends back most of the light.

items.f: TEST IT. Hold a sheet of white paper over a phone torch in a dark room, and look at the top of the paper. What has happened to the light?
items.b: SCATTERED. The paper glows, because the light that gets in is sent out in every direction, and you cannot see the torch's shape.

items.f: TEST IT. At night, with the room light on, look at a clean window pane. You see yourself faintly in it. Which fate of light shows you your face?
items.b: BOUNCES. A small share of the light, about one twelfth, bounces back from the glass and makes a faint mirror.

items.f: TEST IT. Put a pinch of sugar candy powder and a lump of the candy side by side on a black plate. What happens to most of the light in the powder?
items.b: SCATTERED. The lump is clear, and the powder looks white, because its many tiny crystals send the light in all directions.

items.f: TEST IT. Put one drop of cooking oil on a pinch of sugar powder on a black plate. What happens to the light in the oiled patch?
items.b: PASSES ON. The oil fills the gaps between the grains, so the light bends less, and more of it goes through. The patch looks darker and more see-through.

printables.title: Four playing mats
items: BOUNCES: most of the light goes back the way it came, like off a mirror
SOAKED UP: most of the light is taken in by the material and turns into warmth
SCATTERED: most of the light goes off in every direction, so the thing looks white or glows
PASSES ON: most of the light goes straight through to the other side

rules: Cut out the 24 cards and the 4 mats. Take the practice card out and put it to one side. Shuffle the other 23 cards and make a pile, face down. Lay the four mats on the floor. Put the tokens in a bowl.
One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front out loud. The reader keeps the back hidden. After each card, the next player becomes the reader.
Everyone else decides which mat has most of the light. Each player puts one token face down on that mat, without showing the others.
Turn the tokens over together. Then each player says in one sentence why, using the words bounce, soak, scatter or pass.
The reader reads the back. Every player who picked the right mat wins two tokens from the bowl. A player who picked the wrong mat but gave a good reason wins one token.
If the card is a TEST IT card, everyone does the test first. Then pick the mat as usual.

When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins. If you play alone, you are the reader and the player. Put the card on a mat, check the back, and score two for every right answer. Try to beat your score next time. With more than two players, the 20 tokens may run out, so keep score on paper. If a TEST IT card cannot be done (for example, no dark window at night), read the back and talk about it.

flow.do: Cut out the cards, the mats and the tokens. Lay the mats on the floor. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. Put the tokens in a bowl. For TEST IT cards, keep a black plate, a torch, white paper, oil and candy nearby. Crush some candy to powder earlier. Table sugar will do.
flow.say: Every card shows light meeting something. For each card, we decide where most of the light goes. It can bounce, be soaked up, be scattered, or pass on.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and mats. Lay out the mats. Shuffle the cards. Put them face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of the game Where Did the Light Go. You set it up.
flow.parent: Remind your child of the four fates in one sentence each. Bounce is like a mirror. Soaked up is like black cloth. Scattered is like paper or milk. Passes on is like clean glass. The mats have these written on them.

flow.do: Take the practice card. Read the front out loud. Ask your child to choose a mat and say why. Then read the back. Put the card on its mat. Nobody wins a token.
flow.say: Let's practise. Sunlight falls on a clean glass window. Where does most of the light go? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Practice card. Sunlight falls on a clean window. Where does most of the light go?

check.q: Sunlight falls on a clean glass window. Where does most of the light go?
options: It passes on through the glass
It bounces back
It is soaked up
It is scattered
check.why: A clean window passes on about nine tenths of the light. Choosing bounces back usually comes from seeing a faint picture of the room in a window at night, but that is only a small share. Choosing soaked up would make the window dark.

flow.context: In this step, you play the practice card together to learn how the game works.

flow.do: Play the main part. Take turns being the reader. Everyone else puts a token on a mat, face down. Turn them over, give reasons, and read the back. Give tokens as the rules say.
flow.say: Read the front only. Everyone else, put a token on a mat and keep it hidden. Turn them over together. Now tell us why. Then the reader reads the back.
flow.kid: Take turns to read. Put a token on a mat. Turn them over together. Say why.
flow.parent: A good reason uses one of the four words. The sea cards and the sugar cards are the hardest. If your child is stuck, ask what would be left if the light passed on straight through. White things scatter, black things soak up, and mirrors bounce.

ask.q: What do the cards on the SCATTERED mat have in common?
good: They all look white or glow.
They are made of many tiny pieces, such as crystals, drops or fibres.
You cannot see a clear picture through them.

flow.context: In this step, you play the main part of the game, taking turns as the reader.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first. Then try it, and choose the mat.
flow.say: A TEST IT card. Before we try it, everyone say what you think will happen and why. Then we look.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card. First guess what will happen. Why? Then try it.

ask.q: The sugar powder is white, but the lump of candy is clear. What changed?
good: The powder has many surfaces that scatter the light.
Light zigzags through the tiny crystals and comes out in all directions.
Nothing about the sugar changed, only how it is broken up.

flow.think: A drop of oil made the sugar patch darker. What did the oil do to the many surfaces?
flow.context: In this step, you try one of the TEST IT cards together.

flow.do: Count the tokens to find the winner. Then look at the four mats together. Choose one thing from each mat that you can find at home.
flow.say: Let's count the tokens. Then let's look at the four mats. Can you find one thing at home for each?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Who won? Find one thing at home for each mat.
flow.think: Is there anything that sits on two mats at once?
flow.context: In this step, you finish the game and look for the four fates of light at home.

experiments.title: The Vanishing Glass: where does a clear thing go?
experiments.question: A clear glass marble is easy to see in the air. How easy is it to see in water, in cooking oil and in honey? In which liquid does it nearly vanish, and why?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. In which liquid will the marble be hardest to see: water, oil or honey? Which will be easiest? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same marble, the same size of clear glass, the same printed page behind and the same light every time. You look from the same place. Only the liquid changes. You judge each liquid twice, using the same five-point scale, because one look can be a fluke.
results_table: How easy is it to see? (5 = very easy, 1 = nearly vanished)
Can you still see its edge, or a faint ring?
Can you read the printed letters through it?

materials.item: 4 plain clear glasses or small jars of the same size, straight-sided, each holding about 150 millilitres (the marble must be covered by at least 3 centimetres of liquid)
1 clear glass marble without swirls or bubbles inside (a plain clear one is best)
about 120 millilitres of plain water
about 120 millilitres of clear cooking oil, such as refined sunflower or groundnut oil (not coconut oil, which sets in cool weather)

about 120 millilitres of runny, clear honey (a small bottle, about Rs 60 to 100; honey is not for children under one year, and it can be reused in the Find the Marble activity). If you have none, a very thick sugar syrup works less well
a page with a line of large printed letters, a spoon, a torch, a towel and a small tray to work over

experiments.safety: Keep marbles away from children under five, who may put them in their mouths. Do not eat the oil or honey used in the test, and do not give honey to a child under one year old. Work over a tray, because oil makes floors slippery. Wash the marble and glasses with warm water and washing-up liquid afterwards.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the marble in each of the four glasses, as it looked. Last, write what you think, what you saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how easy the marble was to see (5 = very easy, 1 = nearly vanished)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be a little different. The marble should be easiest to see in air and hardest to see in honey.

experiments.context: In this experiment, you put the same clear glass marble in air, water, cooking oil and honey, and find out how easy it is to see in each. You find out what we are really seeing when we see a clear thing.
