setup.art: A hand lowering a clear glass marble on a spoon gently into a glass of water, with letters on a page behind the glass.
setup.caption: 2. Lower the marble gently into the first glass.

setup.art: The marble sitting in a glass of cooking oil, fainter than in water, with the printed letters behind it a little bent.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the marble in the oil. Score how easy it is to see.

setup.art: The marble in a glass of honey, nearly invisible, with only a very faint ring, and the printed letters behind it almost unbent.
setup.caption: 4. Look at the marble in the honey. It almost vanishes.

flow.do: Show your child the marble, the glasses and the three liquids. Ask for a guess about which liquid will hide the marble best, and why. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We have a clear marble and three clear liquids: water, oil and honey. In which one will the marble be hardest to see? Which will be easiest? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A clear marble in three clear liquids. Where is it hardest to see? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the marble might be hard to see in one liquid?
good: The liquid is thick and covers it.
The liquid is clear too, so they blend together.
The liquid is the same kind of see-through as the marble.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start. Write down both. Many children guess honey because it is thick, and some guess water because it is the clearest.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Vanishing Glass experiment. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Set the tray on a table in front of a bright window. Stand the printed page upright behind the tray. Fill one glass with water, one with oil and one with honey, each to about the same height. Leave the fourth glass empty. Mark the four glasses with a label.
flow.say: Pour the water into the first glass, the oil into the second, and the honey into the third. Leave the fourth empty, which is the air test. Stand them in a row, in front of the page.
flow.kid: Fill three glasses with water, oil and honey. Leave one empty. Put the page behind.
flow.parent: Honey is slow to pour. A grown-up can warm the jar in a bowl of warm water for a few minutes, not hot, if it will not flow. Fill all glasses to the same height, about three quarters full. Do the test near a window, so the light is the same for every glass. One child alone does all four glasses. With two to four children, each child pours and scores one liquid, then everyone looks at every glass and scores alone before comparing. Scores will differ by a point or two, and that is fine.
flow.context: In this step, you set out the four glasses and the page that you will look through.

flow.do: Put the marble into the empty glass. Look from the side, at the height of the marble, and score how easy it is to see. Try to read the letters through it. Then lower the marble gently, on a spoon, into the water. Look again, score it, and write down what you see.
flow.say: First the marble in the air. How easy is it to see? Score it out of five. Then lower it into the water. Is it easier or harder to see? What do the letters behind it do?
flow.kid: Look at the marble in the empty glass. Score it. Then put it in water. Score it again.

check.q: In water, the marble is still easy to see, but a little less than in the air. What does this tell you about water and glass?
options: Water bends light a little less than glass does, so there is still a bend at the marble's edge
Water hides things completely
Water soaks up the light
The marble gets smaller in water
check.why: Water bends light by an amount that is different from glass, but not by a lot. So at the marble's edge, light still bends, and your eye can see where the marble is. Choosing that water soaks up the light is a common idea, but a thin layer of clear water soaks up almost nothing.

flow.context: In this step, you look at the marble in air and then in water.

flow.do: Lift the marble out with the spoon, and wipe it dry. Lower it gently into the oil. Look, score it, and try to read the letters. Wipe it again. Lower it into the honey, using the spoon, and push it a little way down. Look, score it, and try to read the letters. Shine the torch at the honey glass from the side and look again.
flow.say: Now the oil. How easy is the marble to see? Now the honey. What happens? Shine a torch from the side. Can you find a faint ring or a glint?
flow.kid: Put the marble in oil. Score it. Then put it in honey. Score it. Shine a torch from the side.

ask.q: In which liquid was the marble hardest to see? What do you notice about the edge?
good: In honey. I could hardly see the edge.
In honey, there was only a faint ring left.
The honey and the glass seem to bend light the same way.

flow.parent: Expected: in oil the marble is much fainter than in water. In honey it almost vanishes, leaving a faint ring, and perhaps a few bubbles or scratches that stay visible. Cheap marbles are made of slightly different glass, so the result varies. If the marble does not nearly vanish, look for a plain one with no swirl. Always let bubbles in the honey rise before you look (this can take a few minutes, so stir gently, not fast). Honey brands differ, and thin honey that has been thinned with sugar syrup hides the marble less well. Even if the marble only fades a lot, the order of air, water, oil, honey is the result that matters. If it does not fade at all, the marble is probably tinted or not glass, so try another.
flow.context: In this step, you put the marble in oil and in honey, and watch it nearly vanish.

flow.do: Fill in the table with your scores. Draw the marble in the four glasses. Compare with your guess.
flow.say: Look at your table. In which liquid was the marble hardest to see? In which was it easiest? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Draw the marble in each glass. Was your guess right?

check.q: The marble almost vanished in honey. What does this tell you about how we see the marble in the air?
options: We see it because light bends and bounces at its edge, where glass meets air
We see it because it is heavy
We see it because it is shiny
We see it because it makes its own light
check.why: Glass and air bend light by very different amounts, so the edge of the marble bends and bounces light, and we see that. In honey the difference is tiny, so there is almost nothing to see. Choosing shiny is close, because shine comes from bouncing light, but the edge bend is the main thing.

flow.context: In this step, you record your results and think about what they mean.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Write it under the drawing.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think at the start? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What is your claim, your evidence and your reasoning?
good: The marble is hardest to see in honey. In honey I could hardly see its edge. Honey and glass bend light about the same, so there is no bend to see.
We see clear things by how they bend light at the edge. If nothing bends, we cannot see them.
The marble did not change. Only the liquid around it did.

flow.parent: A strong answer uses their own scores, says honey (or whichever liquid they found), and links it to bending at the edge. If their results differ, ask what could be different about their marble or liquid.
flow.think: The marble is still in the honey, and nothing about it has changed. Is it still there if you cannot see it?
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist: what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.title: Two Gates for Light: when two see-through filters make darkness
experiments.question: One polarising lens is see-through. What happens when you look through two of them, and turn one of them round?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you look through two sunglass lenses at a bright window, and turn one lens a quarter turn, what will you see? Will it get brighter, darker or stay the same? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: You use the same bright window, the same two lenses and the same distance each time. Only the angle between the two lenses changes. You look at each angle twice and score the brightness out of five, because one look can be a fluke.
results_table: How the two lenses are turned
How bright is the window? (5 = bright, 1 = nearly black)

materials.item: two pairs of polarising sunglasses, or two squares of polarising film. Polarising sunglasses often say polarised on the label or the arm, but many cheap ones sold on the roadside are only dark, so check with the screen test in step 2 before you trust them. A small sheet of polarising film from an optical or hobby shop (about Rs 100 to 200) is the sure choice
a bright window or a white wall in daylight
a laptop, tablet or phone with a bright white screen, for the screen test
a pencil and a table for a recording sheet

experiments.safety: Never look at the Sun through the lenses. Do not use the sunglasses to look at the Sun at all. Hold the lenses by the frame and give borrowed ones back unscratched.
experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw two lenses with their gates, one with upright lines and one with sideways lines, and show a wiggle of light going through the first and being stopped by the second. Last, write what you think, what you saw, and why.
experiments.context: In this experiment, you look through two polarising lenses at a bright window and turn one of them. You find that two see-through lenses can make darkness, and learn that light has a wiggle direction.

setup.art: A child holding a pair of sunglasses up to a laptop screen that is white and bright, then turning the glasses on their side so that the screen goes black.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a screen through sunglasses. Turn them on their side.

setup.art: Two sunglass lenses held one in front of the other, in front of a bright window, with the window looking dim but clear.
setup.caption: 2. Hold two lenses with their arms the same way. The window is dim, but you can see it.

setup.art: The same two lenses with one turned a quarter turn, so that the window becomes dark through the crossed lenses.
setup.caption: 3. Turn one lens a quarter turn. The window goes dark.

setup.art: A third lens held at a slant between two crossed lenses, with the window glowing again through all three.
setup.caption: 4. Put a third lens between them, at an angle. Light comes back.

flow.do: Show your child the sunglasses and the window. Ask for a guess about what will happen when two lenses are crossed. Write the guess at the top of the table.
flow.say: We have two sunglass lenses. Each one is see-through. If I hold one in front of the other, and turn one, what will you see? Brighter, darker or the same? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Two see-through lenses. Turn one. Will the window get darker? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think turning a lens might change the brightness?
good: The lens might only let light through one way.
Turning it changes how much light gets through.
It will not change, because the lens is the same.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any guess with a reason is a good start.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Two Gates for Light experiment. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Check that the sunglasses are polarising. Open a laptop or tablet to a bright white page. Hold one lens in front of your eye and look at the screen. Turn the lens slowly all the way round. If the screen goes dark at one angle, the lens is polarising. Then look at the bright window through one lens, and turn it.
flow.say: Hold the lens to your eye and look at the screen. Turn the lens slowly. Does the screen go dark at some angle? Now look at the window through one lens, and turn it. What happens?
flow.kid: Look at a bright screen through one lens. Turn the lens round. What happens?

ask.q: What happened to the screen when you turned the lens? What happened to the window?
good: The screen went dark at one angle and bright at another.
The window stayed the same brightness when I turned the lens.
The screen's light has a direction, and the window's light does not.

flow.parent: A laptop or tablet screen sends out polarised light, so it goes dark when the lens is turned a quarter turn. The window's light is mostly mixed up in every direction, so turning the lens changes it very little (blue sky can change a little, and so can glare off glass or water, which is fine). If the screen does not go dark, try the other lens. A lens that never changes the screen is not polarising, so do not use it for the next steps. Some phone screens do not work for this test, and some sunglasses are not polarising. Use two lenses that both change the screen.

check.q: The screen went dark when you turned the lens, but the window did not. What does this show?
options: The screen's light wiggles in one direction, and the window's light wiggles in every direction
The screen is brighter than the window
The lens is broken
The window is not a light source
check.why: A polarising lens lets through only light that wiggles in one direction. A screen sends out light that wiggles in one direction, so the lens either lets it through or blocks it. Sunlight from a window wiggles in every direction, so the lens always lets some through.

flow.context: In this step, you test your lenses on a screen and on a window, to see that they are polarising.

flow.do: Hold the two lenses together, one behind the other, in front of the bright window, with their arms pointing the same way. Look through both. Score how bright the window is. Now turn one lens slowly, a quarter of a turn. Stop at halfway and again at a quarter turn. Score the brightness each time. Write them in the table.
flow.say: Hold both lenses together, arms the same way. How bright is the window? Now turn one lens a little. Then a quarter turn. What happens to the brightness?
flow.kid: Hold both lenses up to the window. Turn one slowly. Watch it go dark.

ask.q: What did the two lenses do together, when one was turned a quarter turn?
good: They made the window nearly black.
The window went dark, even though each lens is see-through.
When they were turned, they blocked the light.

flow.parent: With the lenses lined up, the window looks dim but clear, like looking through very dark sunglasses. At a quarter turn, the window goes very dark, typically almost black, perhaps with a purple or blue tint (cheap or curved lenses leave a little light). Halfway between, it is somewhere in the middle. With one child, hold one lens in each hand. With two to four children, one holds the fixed lens, one turns the other and calls out the angle, and one scores the brightness. Swap roles for each angle so everyone scores. Each child's own scores count. Turn all the way round and the window goes bright, dark, bright and dark again, twice each.

check.q: Two lenses that are each see-through gave darkness when one was turned a quarter turn. Why?
options: The first lens lets through only up-and-down wiggles, and the second lets through only side-to-side wiggles, so nothing is left
The lenses soaked up all the light
The lenses were too close together
The window got dimmer
check.why: The first lens passes only wiggles in one direction. The second, turned across it, passes only wiggles in the other direction. None of the first lens's light can get through the second. Choosing that they soaked up all the light misses that each lens alone lets plenty through.

flow.context: In this step, you stack two lenses and turn one, and watch the window go dark.

flow.do: Take a third lens, from the other pair or a spare piece of film. Hold two lenses crossed, so that the window is dark. Slide the third lens between them, and hold it at a slant, halfway between the other two. Look at the window again. Score the brightness. Turn the third lens and see what changes.
flow.say: Keep the two lenses crossed, so the window is dark. Now slide a third lens between them, at an angle. What happens? Is it darker or lighter?
flow.kid: Cross two lenses. Slide a third between. Hold it at a slant. Does light come back?

ask.q: What did the third lens do to the darkness? Does this seem strange?
good: The light came back, even though I added another dark lens.
It seems strange. I added something dark, and it got brighter.
The third lens turned the wiggle halfway, so some can get through the last one.

flow.parent: Optional. This step needs a third lens, such as the other lens from the second pair, held at an angle. It works best when the third lens is turned halfway between the two crossed ones. The light that comes back is dim. The third lens turns the direction of the wiggle partway, so the last lens can pass a part of it. Two pairs of sunglasses give four lenses, so a third is easy to find. Skip this step if you only have two lenses. The light that comes back is dim but clear against the dark, so hold it near a very bright window and be patient.
flow.think: Adding a third see-through lens made the dark window brighter. What does that say about how the filters work?
flow.context: In this step, you try an optional trick: a third lens between two crossed lenses.

flow.do: Fill in the table with your scores. Draw the gates. Compare with the guess from the start.
flow.say: Look at your table. When was the window brightest? When was it darkest? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Fill in the table. Draw the two gates. Was your guess right?
flow.context: In this step, you record your results and draw the gates.

flow.do: Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why. Write it under the drawing.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What did you think at the start? What did you see? Why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Say what you thought, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: What is your claim, your evidence and your reasoning?
good: Two see-through lenses made darkness when one was turned. Each lens lets through light that wiggles one way, so crossed lenses let nothing through.
The window was dark when the lenses were crossed and dim when they were lined up. Light has a wiggle direction, and a filter works like a gate.
A lens can be see-through for one kind of light and opaque for another.

flow.parent: A strong answer says that crossing the lenses gave darkness, and links it to the wiggle direction of light. Ask your child to say whether the lens is see-through or not, and let them find that it depends on the light.
flow.think: Is a polarising lens see-through or opaque? Or does it depend on the light?
flow.context: In this step, you finish like a scientist: what you think, what you saw, and why.

activities.title: Clear Candy, White Powder

materials.item: a few lumps of the clearest rock sugar candy you can find (kalkandu or mishri, about Rs 20 to 40; some is cloudy or white already, so pick pieces you can see through), or large clear sugar crystals
a strong zip bag or two layers of a clean cloth, and a rolling pin
a black or dark plate, and a white plate
a few drops of cooking oil and a small spoon
a sheet of paper with one large printed or thickly pen-written word on it
a phone torch or small torch

schedule.what: Look at the clear candy. Crush it to powder. Compare. Put a drop of oil on the powder, and explain what you see.

activities.record: A drawing of a lump of candy and a heap of powder side by side, with a ray of light zigzagging through each. A sentence on why the powder looks white. A sentence on what the oil did.
activities.safety: Wrap the candy in a cloth or put it in a zip bag before crushing, so no sharp bits fly. Do the crushing on a firm table, with a grown-up nearby, and keep fingers away from the rolling pin. Do not give hard candy to children under five. Do not eat the crushed candy that has had oil on it.
activities.context: In this activity, you crush clear sugar candy into powder and watch it turn white. Then you add a drop of oil to find out what makes the powder see-through again.

setup.art: A hand holding up a clear lump of rock sugar candy to a window, with light shining through it, beside a pile of white sugar powder on a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Look at a lump of clear rock sugar candy. Hold it up to the light.

setup.art: A child gently rolling a rolling pin over a zip bag of crushed sugar candy on a table.
setup.caption: 2. Crush the candy inside a zip bag until it is powder.

setup.art: A pinch of white sugar powder on a black plate with one drop of cooking oil in the middle, making a darker, see-through patch.
setup.caption: 3. Put one drop of oil on a pinch of the powder. The patch darkens.

flow.do: Hold up a lump of the candy to a window or a torch. Describe it. Ask your child what colour the candy would be if it was ground to powder. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: Look at this lump of sugar candy. Is it clear or white? Hold it to the light. What do you think will happen if we crush it into powder? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the candy. Is it clear? What will powder look like? Why?

ask.q: What colour do you think the powder will be? Why do you think so?
good: White, because sugar powder is white.
Clear, because the pieces are clear.
It will be white, because lots of small pieces do something to the light.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say clear, and many say white. Both are good guesses to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of Clear Candy, White Powder. You guess before you crush.

flow.do: Put two lumps of candy in the zip bag, and close it. Lay the bag on a firm table, with a cloth over it. Roll or tap the pin firmly over the bag until the candy is a coarse powder (kalkandu is hard, so this takes a few minutes, and a heavy steel tumbler base or a pestle also works). Children take turns, with the grown-up holding the bag. Pour a pinch of the powder onto the white plate, and another pinch onto the black plate. Put a whole lump next to each.
flow.say: Put the candy in the bag. Roll the pin over it until it is powder. Now tip a pinch onto each plate. Which looks clear, and which looks white?
flow.kid: Put the candy in a bag. Roll it flat. Tip a pinch onto each plate.
flow.parent: A grown-up should help with the rolling pin. Crush until most of the candy is a fine powder. On the black plate, the powder will look strikingly white, while the lump looks clear or yellowish. Hold the plates in sunlight or under a bright light.

check.q: The lump of candy is clear, but the powder is white. What changed?
options: Crushing made many tiny surfaces that scatter light in every direction
The sugar changed into a white material
The sugar soaked up more light
The powder is heavier
check.why: Each grain is still clear. But the powder has thousands of surfaces, and light bends and bounces at every one, so it zigzags through the heap and comes back out in all directions. Mixed light from every direction looks white. Choosing that the sugar changed is a common idea, but the sugar is the same.

flow.context: In this step, you crush the candy into powder, and compare the lump with the powder.

flow.do: Spread a thin, even layer of powder over the printed word on the paper. Can you still read the word? Now put 2 or 3 drops of cooking oil on half of the layer and spread them with the spoon. Watch what happens to the white. Can you read the word under the oiled half and not under the dry half? Shine the torch from the side, and look at both halves. Each child can try a heap of their own on a black plate.
flow.say: Put one drop of oil on the powder. What happens to the white? Is the oiled patch lighter or darker? Which one lets you see the plate?
flow.kid: Put a drop of oil on the powder. What happens to the white?

ask.q: Why do you think the oil made the white powder look darker?
good: The oil fills the gaps between the grains, so the light bends less and goes through.
The oil makes the sugar more see-through.
The oil is like the honey, bending light the same as sugar.

flow.parent: The oiled patch looks darker and a bit see-through, because oil bends light by an amount that is closer to sugar than air does. If nothing seems to happen, use more oil and spread it until the grains are wet all through, because a single drop only wets a small spot. The change is clear but not complete, because oil and sugar do not match exactly. This is the same idea as the marble in honey.
flow.context: In this step, you add a drop of oil to the powder and watch the white fade.

flow.do: Draw the lump and the heap of powder side by side. Draw the light zigzagging in the powder. Write a sentence on why the powder is white, and why oil made it darker.
flow.say: Draw the lump and the powder. Show the light zigzagging through the powder. Then write why the powder is white, and why the oil changed it.
flow.kid: Draw a lump and a heap. Draw a zigzag of light in the heap.
flow.think: Snow is made of clear ice crystals, and looks white. When snow melts, it looks clear. Why?
flow.context: In this step, you draw what you saw and explain it.

activities.title: Ten Light Balls: act out the four fates

materials.item: 16 soft balls, or 16 rolled-up socks or paper balls, to be the light

2 or more players: one throws, and one plays each material in turn (the 'material' can be one person holding up a prop: a hand-sized foil card for the mirror, a black cloth, a sheet of butter paper or a rough white sheet, and a plain open frame or a clear plastic sheet for the window). With 3 or 4 players, each plays one material.
a bowl or basket on the far side of a room, to catch the light that gets through
paper and a pencil to keep score

schedule.what: Act out the four fates of light. Count how many of 16 balls pass through two, three and four half-lenses in a row.

activities.record: A table with four rows, one for each material, and columns for how many balls bounced, were soaked up, were scattered and passed on. A sentence on how many of 16 balls get through two, three and four half-lenses in a row.
activities.safety: Use soft balls or socks only, and throw gently, below chest height and never at faces. Use a foil card for the mirror, never real glass. Clear the room of things that can break.
activities.context: In this activity, you and your family act out what happens to light. One person throws ten soft balls, and others play a window, a mirror, a black cloth and a frosted pane, to see where the light goes.

setup.art: A room with a child throwing soft balls at four people standing in a line: one holding a clear sheet, one a mirror, one a black cloth, and one a rough white sheet.
setup.caption: 1. One person throws the balls. Each other person plays one material.

setup.art: A child playing a window, holding up a clear sheet and letting nine balls fly past her but catching and throwing back one.
setup.caption: 2. A window lets nine of ten balls past, and bounces one back.

setup.art: Two children standing one behind the other as two windows, with balls passing through the first and some stopping at the second, and a basket at the end.
setup.caption: 3. Put two windows in a row. Count how many balls get through both.

flow.do: Choose roles. One person is the Sun and throws ten balls. Others are the materials: a mirror, a black cloth, a frosted pane and a window. Explain what each material does with a ball. Practise once.
flow.say: I will throw ten balls of light. The mirror throws every ball back. The black cloth catches every ball and keeps it. The frosted pane throws each ball in a random direction. The window lets balls past, but bounces one back.
flow.kid: One person throws the balls. The others are a mirror, a black cloth, a frosted pane and a window.

ask.q: What do you think will happen to light when it meets each of these?
good: The mirror sends it back, and the black cloth soaks it up.
The frosted pane will send it everywhere.
The window will let most through.

flow.parent: Two people are enough: your child throws and you play each material in turn, then swap. With three or four children, one throws, one counts and writes, and the others are the materials, and everyone swaps after each material. The mirror may catch the ball and throw it back at the Sun. The frosted pane turns the player round and throws the ball in a random direction.
flow.context: This is the first step of Ten Light Balls. You choose who plays what.

flow.do: Throw ten balls at each material in turn. Count how many bounced back, how many were kept, how many were thrown about in random directions and how many passed through. Write them in the table. For the window, let nine balls past and bounce one back.
flow.say: Throw ten balls at the mirror. How many bounce back? Now the black cloth. Now the frosted pane. Now the window. Write each number in the table.
flow.kid: Throw ten balls at each. Count how many bounce, stay, scatter and pass.

check.q: For each material, the numbers in the table add up to ten. Why?
options: Every ball must go somewhere, so the four shares add up to all ten
Because we always throw ten
Because ten is a nice number
Because balls cannot be lost
check.why: Each ball bounces, is kept, scatters or passes on. There are no other choices. So the four counts must add up to ten. In real life, the four shares of light also add up to all of the light that fell.

flow.context: In this step, you throw the balls at each material and count where they go.

flow.do: Now use dark sunglass lenses that pass half the light: the player catches every second ball and lets the others go past. Put two of them in a row (use two players, or one player who stands in two places). Throw 16 balls at the first. Count how many get through. Then throw only those through the second. Count again. Write the numbers. Try three and four lenses in a row.
flow.say: Put two sunglass lenses in a row. Sixteen balls hit the first. Every second ball gets through, so eight get past. Now those eight hit the second lens. How many get through? Half of eight is four.
flow.kid: Two windows in a row. Count how many balls get through both.

ask.q: Does the second lens take away the same number of balls as the first, or the same share of what reached it?
good: The same share. The first took 8 and the second took only 4.
Each lens lets through half of what comes in.
Each window takes the same share, not the same number.

flow.parent: The point is that each lens passes the same share, not the same number. 16 balls become 8, then 4, then 2, then 1. If you want a clear window instead, nine tenths is hard to act out with whole balls: 10 becomes 9, then about 8, then about 7. A bowl on the far side counts the balls that make it. The pattern is exact only because you follow the rule, so say that this is a pretend light.
flow.think: If every window takes one tenth of what reaches it, will light ever reach zero?
flow.context: In this step, you put two and three windows in a row and see how the light fades.

activities.title: Find the Marble: three ways to catch a hidden clear thing

materials.item: a clear glass marble in a glass jar of honey, left from the Vanishing Glass test
a torch or phone torch
a page with a pattern of straight lines drawn on it with a thick pen, such as a set of parallel stripes
a polarising lens or a pair of polarising sunglasses, and a laptop screen with a white page (optional)
a towel and a spoon

schedule.what: Try three ways to find the hidden marble in the honey: change the light, change the background, and look through a polarising lens.

activities.record: A table of three ways to find the hidden marble, with a tick for the ones that worked and a sentence on how you think each one works.
activities.safety: Keep marbles away from children under five. Do not give honey to a child under one year old. Wipe up spills at once.
activities.context: In this activity, you hide a clear marble in honey, and then try three ways to find it again. You find out what you can do to make a clear thing show up.

setup.art: A glass jar of honey with a clear marble hidden inside, a hand holding a torch beam from the side, and a faint bright ring around the marble.
setup.caption: 1. Shine a torch from the side to catch the marble's edge.

setup.art: The jar of honey standing in front of a page of thick stripes, with the stripes looking bent in a small circle where the marble is.
setup.caption: 2. Put a striped page behind the jar. The stripes bend at the marble.

setup.art: A child looking through a polarising sunglass lens at the jar, with coloured patterns showing inside the marble.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the jar through a polarising lens, with a bright screen behind.

flow.do: Use the jar of honey with the marble inside. Or lower the marble into a jar of honey and let the bubbles rise. Ask your child how they could find the marble without touching it. Write down the ideas.
flow.say: The marble is hidden in the honey. How could you find it without touching it? Think of three ways. Why do you think they would work?
flow.kid: A marble is hidden in honey. How can you find it without touching?

ask.q: What could you change to make a clear thing show up?
good: Change the light, for example shine a torch from the side.
Put something with a pattern behind it.
Look at it in a different way.

flow.parent: Do not correct the ideas. Lead with the idea that we see clear things by what they do to light, so each idea should change what the light does.
flow.context: This is the first step of Find the Marble. You think of ways to find a hidden clear thing.

flow.do: In a dim room, hold the torch to the side of the jar, level with the marble. Move the beam slowly across. Look for a glint or a faint ring. Then stand the striped page behind the jar. Look through the jar at the stripes. Find the place where the stripes bend or break.
flow.say: Shine the torch from the side. Look for a glint where the marble is. Now put the stripes behind the jar. Where do the stripes look bent? That is where the marble is.
flow.kid: Shine a torch from the side. Look for a glint. Put stripes behind the jar.

check.q: The stripes looked bent where the marble was hidden. What does this show?
options: Honey and glass bend light a tiny bit differently, so the marble still bends the stripes slightly
The marble is magic
The stripes are not straight
The honey is a lens
check.why: Honey and glass bend light by almost the same amount, but not exactly. So there is a small bend where they meet. Stripes behind the jar show even a small bend, because the eye can tell when a straight line is broken. Choosing that the honey is a lens misses that the bend is at the marble's edge.

flow.parent: Use the thickest, bubble-free honey jar from the first experiment. If the glint is hard to see, darken the room and tilt the torch a little up or down. Stripes about a finger wide work best, and the jar should stand a hand's width in front of the page. Never shine the torch into anyone's eyes. With several children, one holds the torch, one holds the page, and one looks, then they swap.
flow.context: In this step, you find the marble with a torch from the side, and with stripes behind the jar.

flow.do: Open a laptop to a bright white page, and stand the jar of honey in front of the screen. Hold a polarising lens in front of your eye. Look at the jar through the lens and turn the lens slowly. Look inside the marble for coloured bands or dark patches.
flow.say: Put the jar in front of a bright white screen. Look at the jar through the lens, and turn the lens. Do you see colours or dark patches in the marble?
flow.kid: Put the jar in front of a white screen. Look through the lens and turn it.
flow.parent: Optional. Children can take turns with the lens, one holding the jar and one looking. A glass marble that cooled quickly has stress inside. Between a polarised screen and a polarising lens, stress shows up as coloured bands or a dark cross. Many marbles show nothing, and a screen that is not polarised or a lens that is not polarising shows nothing either, so this step may not work. That is a result too, so write down what you saw. Do the torch and stripes steps first, because they work with every marble.
flow.think: A polarising lens helps to show stress in clear glass and plastic. What else might it help us see?
flow.context: In this step, you look at the marble through a polarising lens, in front of a bright screen.

flow.do: Fill in the table of the three ways. Tick the ones that worked. Write one sentence on how each works.
flow.say: Which ways worked? For each, tell me what it changes about the light.
flow.kid: Which ways found the marble? Why did they work?

ask.q: What did each of the three ways change about what the light was doing?
good: The torch changed the light so the edge caught it.
The stripes showed where the light bent.
The lens showed the direction of the light's wiggle.

flow.context: In this step, you write down which ways worked and why.

projects.title: Tape Stained Glass: colours from clear tape

materials.item: a sheet of clear plastic, such as a clear report cover or a clear plastic folder, about the size of a postcard or larger
a roll of clear, shiny sticky tape, not the frosted kind, and scissors
a polarising lens: a lens from polarising sunglasses, or a square of polarising film
a laptop or tablet screen with a bright white page, or any lit-up white screen that works with your polarising lens
a pencil, a ruler and a piece of paper to draw a plan

schedule.what: Draw a plan. Stick layers of clear tape onto the plastic to make a picture. Look at it through a polarising lens in front of a white screen. Turn the lens and watch the colours change.

projects.record: A drawing of your design, with the number of layers of tape in each part. A note on which number of layers gave which colour. A sentence on what happens when you turn the lens.
projects.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors. Look at the screen only for short spells, in a dim room, and rest your eyes. Keep tape off the screen, and do not stick the tape on it.
projects.context: In this project, you stick layers of clear tape on clear plastic and look at them through a polarising lens. You make colours from clear materials.

setup.art: A sheet of clear plastic on a table with strips of clear tape being stuck in overlapping layers to form a simple flower shape.
setup.caption: 1. Stick strips of clear tape in layers to make a picture.

setup.art: The taped picture laid on a bright white laptop screen in a dim room.
setup.caption: 2. Lay the picture on a white screen.

setup.art: A child holding a polarising lens in front of her eye, looking at the taped picture, which glows in bright colours of orange, green, purple and blue.
setup.caption: 3. Look at the picture through the polarising lens. Colours appear.

setup.art: The same picture with the lens turned a quarter turn, now showing the opposite colours.
setup.caption: 4. Turn the lens. The colours change.

flow.do: Show your child the clear plastic and the tape. Ask what colour the tape will make, if anything. Write down the guess and the reason.
flow.say: We will stick clear tape on clear plastic. It is all see-through. Do you think it will make any colour? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Clear tape on clear plastic. Will it make any colour? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think clear things might make colours?
good: They will not, because they are clear.
Maybe the tape bends the light.
Maybe layers make colours, like soap bubbles.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people say there will be no colour at all, which is a good prediction to test.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tape Stained Glass project. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Draw a simple design on paper, such as a flower with five petals and a leaf. Plan how many layers of tape will go in each part. Use one layer for some parts, two for others, three for others and four for the rest. Write the plan on the paper.
flow.say: Draw a flower or a pattern. In each part, decide how many layers of tape. One layer here, two layers there, three, four. Write the numbers on your plan.
flow.kid: Draw a flower. Plan 1, 2, 3 or 4 layers of tape for each part.
flow.parent: Different numbers of layers give different colours. Keep each piece of tape lying flat, with no bubbles. Put a small number on each part of your plan so you can match colours to layers later.
flow.context: In this step, you plan your design and decide on the layers.

flow.do: A grown-up helps to cut strips of tape about 3 centimetres long. Stick the strips onto the plastic, in layers, following your plan. Lay each layer across the one below, not in line with it. Press out the bubbles. Stick the first layer for every part, then the second layers, and so on.
flow.say: Stick the first layer of tape for every part. Then the second layer on the parts that need two. Then the third. Press out bubbles. Lay each new strip across the one below.
flow.kid: Cut strips of tape. Stick them on the plastic in layers. Press out bubbles.
flow.parent: The tape does not need to cover the whole sheet. A flower shape in the middle looks best. Cross each layer over the last at a slant, because colours are stronger when the layers lie in different directions. Plain clear tape gives more colour than matt tape. Ordinary cello tape from a stationery shop works; brown or masking tape does not. Each child can make their own small flower, and several children can share one screen and one lens by taking turns.

check.q: Before we look through the polarising lens, the taped picture just looks clear. What will the lens show?
options: It will show colours that depend on the number of layers
It will show nothing
It will show the colour of the tape
It will make the tape disappear
check.why: Clear tape is made of stretched plastic, which turns the direction of the wiggle of light by an amount that depends on its thickness and on the colour. Between a polarised screen and a polarising lens, the turn shows up as colour. Without the lens, you cannot see it.

flow.context: In this step, you stick the layers of tape on the plastic, following your plan.

flow.do: Lay the plastic on the white screen in a dim room. Look at it through the polarising lens. Turn the lens slowly all the way round. Note the colours of each part. Match them to the number of layers. Write them on your plan.
flow.say: Put your picture on the screen. Look at it through the lens. What colours do you see? Turn the lens. Do the colours change? Which number of layers gave which colour?
flow.kid: Lay your picture on the screen. Look through the lens. Turn it. What colours?

ask.q: Why does turning the lens change the colours?
good: The lens lets through light that wiggles in one direction only, so turning it picks different colours.
The tape turns the wiggle by different amounts for different colours.
Different layers turn the light by different amounts.

flow.parent: If you see no colours, check that the screen is polarising by turning the lens and seeing that the screen goes dark at one angle. Some phone screens do not work for this. Use a laptop or tablet screen if you can. Turn the plastic sheet itself on the screen too, because the colours are strongest when the tape lies at a slant, about halfway between the screen's dark and bright angles. One layer may look only pale grey or cream, and more layers give stronger colours, so if you see nothing, try five or six layers. If the bare plastic sheet itself shows colour, that is stress in the plastic, so compare it with the taped part. Without a polarising lens and screen, you can ask an adult to put the picture in a sunny window and view it through a pair of polarising sunglasses.
flow.think: The tape is clear and shows no colour by itself. Where do the colours come from?
flow.context: In this step, you look at your picture through the lens and watch the colours.

flow.do: Write on your plan what colours each number of layers gave. Write one sentence on what the lens did to the clear tape.
flow.say: Write the colours on your plan. Which number of layers gave which colour? What did the lens help you see?
flow.kid: Write the colours on your plan. What did the lens show?
flow.context: In this step, you record your results and explain what you saw.

challenges.title: Vanish the Marble: make a liquid that hides it best
challenges.problem: A clear glass marble almost vanishes in honey. Cooking oil hides it a lot, and water hardly at all. How close can you get with a cheap sugar syrup? Can a syrup beat oil, or even match honey?
challenges.safety: A grown-up does all the warming of water, and handles anything hot. Syrup that has just been made can scald, so it must be cool before a child touches it. Keep marbles away from children under five. Do not give honey to a child under one year old.
constraints: Use only things from the kitchen: water, sugar, cooking oil and honey. No chemicals.
A grown-up does any warming of water. The syrup must be cool before the marble goes in.
Use the same marble and the same jar for every test.
You must judge each liquid by looking from the side and scoring how easy the marble is to see, out of five.
materials: 5 small clear jars or glasses of the same size, about 150 millilitres (water, thin syrup, thick syrup, oil and honey)
sugar, water, cooking oil and honey
a spoon, a measuring cup and a kettle or pan for a grown-up to warm water
a torch, a page with a line of large print and a pencil for scoring
general: A thin sugar syrup, half a cup of sugar to half a cup of water.

A thick sugar syrup, as much sugar as dissolves in a small cup of warm water, then cooled. A syrup this thick usually bends light a little less than oil and honey do, so expect it to come second or third.
Plain honey, which is the standard to beat. Honey and oil are typically close to each other.
creative: Make three syrups of different thickness and line them up, from thin to thick, to see the marble fade as the syrup gets thicker.
Mix a little warm water into honey, a spoonful at a time, and see whether the marble reappears.
Test other clear things, such as a clear plastic bead or a piece of clear plastic, in the best syrup.
challenges.your_turn: Sketch your plan. Make your syrups, and test each one with the marble. Score each out of five. Which liquid hid the marble best? Did a thicker syrup always hide it better? Why do you think so?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about matching liquids. You try to make a cheap syrup that hides a clear marble as well as honey does.

setup.art: A child sketching a plan on paper with four jars labelled thin syrup, thick syrup, honey and oil.
setup.caption: 1. Sketch your plan and list the liquids to test.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into a measuring cup of sugar, and a child stirring it with a spoon until clear.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up warms water. Stir in sugar until it dissolves. Let it cool.

setup.art: A row of four jars on a tray with a clear marble in each, the marble getting fainter from left to right, as the liquid gets thicker.
setup.caption: 3. Put the marble in each jar. Score how easy it is to see.

flow.do: Read the problem together. Ask your child to guess whether a thicker syrup will hide the marble better, and why. Write down the plan and the guess.
flow.say: Honey hides the marble well. Can we make a syrup from sugar and water that works as well? Will a thicker syrup hide the marble better? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Can sugar syrup hide the marble like honey? Will thicker be better? Why?

ask.q: What do you think makes a liquid good at hiding a glass marble?
good: It must be thick.
It must bend light by the same amount as glass.
It must be clear.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Vanish the Marble challenge. You plan.

flow.do: A grown-up warms 100 millilitres of water until it is warm, not boiling. Stir in sugar a spoonful at a time, until no more will dissolve. Let it cool. Make a second, thinner syrup with half as much sugar. Pour each syrup into its own jar, to the same height. Pour the honey, the oil and plain water into three more jars.
flow.say: A grown-up warms the water. Stir in sugar a spoonful at a time, until no more dissolves. That is your thick syrup. Make a thinner one with half the sugar. Wait until they have cooled.
flow.kid: A grown-up warms water. Stir in sugar until no more dissolves. Let it cool.
flow.parent: Never let a child handle hot water or hot syrup. Warm water is enough, because warm water dissolves more sugar. The thick syrup should flow like slow honey when it is cool. If it sets into crystals, stir in a spoonful of warm water. Let the syrup stand for 10 minutes so that the stirring bubbles rise, because bubbles make the marble easy to see and spoil the test. With two to four children, each makes one syrup (one thick, one thin, one in between) and everyone scores all the jars alone. You need about 150 grams of sugar in all, which costs only a few rupees.
flow.context: In this step, you and a grown-up make the sugar syrups and set up the jars.

flow.do: Put the marble gently into each jar in turn. Let bubbles rise. Look from the side. Score how easy it is to see, out of five, and try to read the print through it. Wipe the marble and go on to the next. Do each jar twice.
flow.say: Put the marble in the thin syrup. Score it. Wipe it and put it in the thick syrup. Score it. Then the honey and the oil. Which hides the marble best?
flow.kid: Put the marble in each jar. Score it out of five. Wipe it between.

check.q: The thick syrup hid the marble better than the thin syrup. Why?
options: The thick syrup bends light by an amount closer to glass, so the edge shows less
The thick syrup is heavier
The thick syrup is darker
The marble sank deeper
check.why: Dissolved sugar makes water bend light more, and the more sugar, the more it bends. A thick syrup bends light closer to glass, so there is less of a bend at the marble's edge, and it nearly vanishes. Heaviness or darkness is not the cause.

flow.context: In this step, you test each liquid with the marble and score how easy it is to see.

flow.do: Compare your scores. Rank the liquids from best to worst at hiding the marble. Write down what you found, and what you would try next.
flow.say: Which liquid hid the marble best? Did the thick syrup match the honey? What would you try next?
flow.kid: Which liquid hid the marble best? What would you try next?

ask.q: Which liquid hid the marble best, and why do you think so?
good: Honey, because it bends light about the same as glass.
The thickest syrup, because more sugar makes water bend light more.
The ones that were thicker were better, but there seems to be a limit.

flow.parent: Typically, honey and oil hide the marble best, then the thick syrup, then the thin syrup, then water. The thick syrup will probably not match honey, and that is a real result, not a failure. Thicker is better up to a point, but a syrup cannot bend light more than the sugar allows. If the marble still shows clearly in all of them, the scores will be close, so look at the edge and the print behind it, not only at the marble. If your results differ, ask what could differ about the jars or the light.
flow.think: Why do you think a thick syrup cannot beat honey?
flow.context: In this step, you rank your liquids and think about what to try next.

items.p: Which of these best describes a translucent material, such as butter paper?
opts: It lets light through, but scatters it, so you see a glow and no clear picture
It lets all light through in straight lines
items.why: A translucent material passes on light but scatters it in many directions. A transparent material lets light through straight, and an opaque one lets none through.

items.p: Every bit of light that meets a material is bounced back, soaked up, scattered or ____ on.
items.why: The four things that can happen to light are bounce, soak up, scatter and pass on. Together the four shares make up all of the light that fell.

items.p: True or false: a clean glass window lets all of the light through.
items.why: False. A clean window passes on about nine tenths of the light. A small share bounces back, which is why you can see yourself faintly in a window at night, and a little is soaked up.

items.p: Out of every 100 parts of light falling on a window pane, 90 parts pass on and 8 parts bounce back. How many parts are soaked up?
items.why: The four shares add up to 100. 90 plus 8 is 98. 100 take away 98 is 2. So 2 parts are soaked up.

items.p: A clear glass marble almost vanishes in honey. What is the best reason?
opts: Honey bends light by almost the same amount as glass does, so there is hardly any bend at the edge to see
items.why: We see a clear thing only where light bends or bounces at its edge. Honey and glass slow light by almost the same amount, so the bend is tiny and the marble nearly disappears. Thickness and colour are not the reason.

items.p: Put the steps of the Vanishing Glass test in order, from first to last.
items: Guess which liquid will hide the marble best, and why
Fill the glasses with water, oil and honey and leave one empty
Look at the marble in the air and in the water, and score each
Look at the marble in the oil and in the honey, and score each
Say what you thought, what you saw and why
items.why: A fair test starts with a guess and a reason. Then you set out the same glasses for every liquid, look at each in turn, and finish by saying what you found out and why.

items.p: Sort these clear things by how easy they are to see. Do they stand out clearly, or nearly vanish?
items: a glass marble in the air
Easy to see
a glass marble in honey
Nearly vanishes
a heat-proof glass rod in cooking oil
Nearly vanishes
a clear plastic bottle on a table
Easy to see
jelly-like water beads in a glass of water
Nearly vanishes
a glass marble in the air against a dark wall
Easy to see
items.why: A clear thing stands out when it bends light at its edge by a different amount from what is around it. It nearly vanishes when the thing around it bends light by almost the same amount.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: transparent
lets light through in straight lines, so you see clearly
translucent
lets light through but scatters it, so you see no clear picture
opaque
lets no visible light through
matching liquid
a liquid that bends light by about the same amount as a clear solid
items.why: These three words describe three ways of sharing out light among bounce, soak, scatter and pass. A matching liquid is the trick that makes a clear thing nearly vanish.

items.p: Rock sugar candy is clear, but ground to powder it is white. Why?
opts: The powder has thousands of tiny surfaces that scatter light in every direction
The sugar changes into a white material when it is crushed
The powder soaks up more light
items.why: Each grain is still clear. But light bends and bounces at every surface and zigzags through the heap, coming back out in all directions. Mixed light from every direction looks white.

items.p: True or false: a heap of clear salt crystals looks white because salt is made of a white material.
items.why: False. Each salt crystal is clear. The heap looks white because the many tiny surfaces scatter light in every direction.

items.p: Polarised light is light whose waves all wiggle in the same ____.
items.why: Ordinary light wiggles in every direction at once. Polarised light wiggles in only one direction, for example only up and down.

items.p: Two sunglass lenses are each see-through. Explain how two of them held together can make darkness.
items.a: Each lens lets through only light that wiggles in one direction. If the lenses are turned a quarter turn from each other, the first lens lets through only up-and-down wiggles and the second lets through only side-to-side wiggles. So nothing can get through both, and it is dark.
items.why: A strong answer says that each lens is like a gate for one wiggle direction, and that gates at right angles block everything.

items.p: Here is a drawing of light falling on a window pane. Label the four things that can happen to the light.
labels: the light that is soaked up
a: the light that bounces back: a small share that goes back toward the room
the light that is soaked up: a very small share that stays in the glass and warms it
the light that is scattered: almost none, because a clean window is smooth
the light that passes on: the biggest share, about nine tenths, which goes straight through
items.why: A clean window passes on most of the light. A small share bounces back and a little is soaked up. A smooth clean window scatters almost none, but frosted glass scatters most of what gets through.
items.art: A beam of light hitting a window pane from the left, with a thick arrow going through, a small arrow bouncing back, a tiny arrow ending inside the glass, and no scattered arrows, and four empty label boxes.

items.p: Draw a heap of clear sugar crystals and a ray of light zigzagging through it and coming out in many directions.
items.a: A heap of many small shapes with a ray going in on one side, bouncing off several faces, and coming back out of the heap in different directions, some at the top and some at the sides.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the ray changing direction many times and leaving the heap going in many directions. That is scattering, and it is why the heap looks white.

items.p: Three children look at a pond and cannot see any fish there.

views.says: There is no fish in the pond, because I can see right to the bottom.
There may be fish that are almost see-through. Clear things are hard to see.
Look for shadows on the bottom, and for dark dots that could be eyes. Clear things still stop a little light.

items.ask: Which child would you trust most? Give a reason from what you know about clear things, and say one thing that you would look for.
items.a: A strong answer picks Kavya or Farhan, and says that clear things are seen by what they do to light, so a clear fish could still make shadows and have dark eyes. It might look for flickering shadows on the pond floor, or look against a dark cloth.
items.why: We see clear things only through what they do to light. A nearly clear animal still has dark eyes, a gut and a backbone, and casts a faint shadow, so Anu's reasoning is too quick.

items.p: A window passes on 9 of every 10 parts of the light. Out of 200 parts of light that fall on it, how many parts pass on?
items.why: A tenth of 200 is 20. Nine tenths is 9 times 20, which is 180. So 180 parts pass on.

items.p: Four identical sunglass lenses are held in a row. Each lets through half of the light that reaches it. What share of the original light gets through all four?
items.why: After the first lens a half is left. After the second, half of a half, which is a quarter. After the third, an eighth. After the fourth, a sixteenth. Each lens takes the same share of what reaches it.

items.p: A made-up lens passes one half of the light that reaches it. 640 parts of light fall on the first of three of these lenses in a row. How many parts get through the third lens?
items.why: Half of 640 is 320. Half of 320 is 160. Half of 160 is 80. So 80 parts get through all three.

items.p: A red fish is 20 metres deep in clear sea water, with only sunlight. The fish looks dark brown or black. What is the best reason?
opts: The water has soaked up most of the red light before it reaches the fish
items.why: Water soaks up red light more than blue, so within about ten metres most of the red is gone. A red fish needs red light to look red. With none left, she looks dark.

items.p: True or false: a red fish deep in the sea is easy to spot with only sunlight.
items.why: False. In the deep, only blue light is left, and a red animal soaks that blue up, so she looks black. This is one way red helps animals hide in deep water.

items.p: Ordinary window glass passes visible light but blocks most ultraviolet B light. What is the best explanation?
opts: Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to lift electrons in the glass, and visible photons do not
Ultraviolet is a colour that glass does not like
Glass is too thin for ultraviolet
items.why: Light comes in packets of energy. Ultraviolet packets carry more energy than visible ones. In glass, only the big packets are strong enough to move the electrons, so the glass soaks up ultraviolet and passes visible light.

items.p: A trace of ____ in clear aluminium oxide turns it into a red ruby.
items.why: Pure aluminium oxide is clear. A tiny amount of chromium gives its electrons a jump that soaks up some colours of light, and the crystal looks red.

items.p: Is each of these mostly stopped by the material, or mostly passed on?
items: visible light meeting a brick wall
Mostly stopped
Wi-Fi radio waves meeting a brick wall
Mostly passes through
X-rays meeting soft parts of a hand
Mostly passes through
X-rays meeting a bone
Mostly stopped
ultraviolet B meeting a window pane
Mostly stopped
neutrinos meeting the Earth
Mostly passes through
items.why: Whether something is opaque depends on the kind of wave. A brick wall stops light but passes many radio waves. Bone stops X-rays and soft parts pass them. Neutrinos pass through almost everything.

items.p: Put the journey of ordinary light through two crossed polarising filters in order.
items: Ordinary light arrives, wiggling in every direction
The first filter lets through only the up-and-down wiggles
The second filter, turned a quarter turn, blocks the up-and-down wiggles
Almost no light comes out of the second filter
items.why: The first filter picks one wiggle direction. The second filter, at right angles, accepts only the other direction. Nothing is left for it to pass, so the world looks dark.

items.p: Match each use of polarised light to what it does.
pairs: polarising sunglasses
cut the glare bouncing off water and wet roads
a bee or a desert ant
uses the pattern of polarised light in the sky as a compass
a dung beetle
keeps a straight line by the polarised light of the Moon
a laptop screen with a polarising lens
goes dark when the lens is turned a quarter turn
items.why: Light that bounces off a flat shiny surface is partly polarised, and so is light from the sky and from many screens. Filters and some animals can sort light by its wiggle direction.

items.p: A wet piece of cloth looks darker than a dry one. What is the best explanation?
opts: Water fills the gaps between the fibres, so less light is scattered back to your eye
items.why: Dry cloth scatters light at the many surfaces between fibres and air. Water fills the gaps and bends light less at each surface, so less light scatters back to your eye, and the cloth looks darker.

items.p: Explain why an eye that let all the light pass through it, without stopping any, could not see.
items.a: An eye senses light by soaking some of it up. Special cells at the back take in the light and send a signal to the brain. If the light all passed through, the cells would have nothing to sense. That is why almost every see-through animal still has dark eyes.
items.why: A strong answer says that seeing needs the eye to take in some light. A perfectly see-through eye would pass the light on, and the animal would sense nothing.

items.p: Draw three windows in a row, each passing on nine tenths of the light. Write the share left after each one, starting from 100.
items.a: Three panes in a row with arrows between them, labelled 100, 90, 81 and about 73.
items.why: Each window takes one tenth of what reaches it. 100 becomes 90, then 81, then about 73. The light fades in steps, and each step is a smaller loss.

items.p: A family is buying sunglasses for a child.

views.says: Buy the darkest pair. The darker they are, the more they protect her eyes.
Check the label first. What matters is whether the lenses block ultraviolet, whatever the colour.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from what you know about light, and say what you would check in the shop.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the aunt. Dark lenses with no ultraviolet filter make the pupils open wider, so more ultraviolet can enter the eye. The shopper should check for a label that says the lenses block ultraviolet.
items.why: The darkness of a lens and its ultraviolet filter are different things. A dark lens with no filter can let in more ultraviolet, because the pupil opens wide behind it.

items.p: About 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimetre of your skin each second, and you feel nothing. What does this show?
opts: Almost no neutrinos are stopped by your body
Your skin is made of glass
items.why: If your body stopped a share of them, they would warm you or be detected. Almost all pass through, and only a very tiny number are stopped. So a person is nearly see-through to neutrinos.

items.p: Here is a drawing of the Vanishing Glass test, with a marble in a glass of honey. Label four parts.
labels: the faint ring at the marble's edge
a: the honey: bends light by almost the same amount as glass
the faint ring at the marble's edge: where a tiny bend is left
the printed page behind: its letters hardly bend as they pass the marble
items.why: The ring is the last trace of the marble, where honey and glass do not match exactly. The page behind shows how little light bends at the marble's edge.
items.art: A glass jar of honey with a clear marble almost invisible inside, a faint ring around the marble, and a printed page standing behind the jar, with four empty label boxes.

items.p: Three of these are clear to light. Which one is the odd one out?
opts: A lump of clear rock sugar candy
A heap of sugar candy powder
items.why: The powder is made of the same clear sugar, but its many surfaces scatter light in every direction, so the heap looks white and you cannot see through it. The other three let light pass on straight.

items.p: In clear sea water at 50 metres deep, which colour of sunlight is left the most?
items.why: Water soaks up red first, then orange, yellow and green. Blue is soaked up least, so blue is the colour that lasts the deepest.

items.p: Two identical windows are in a row. Each passes on 90 parts of every 100. What share of the light passes through both?
items.why: The first window passes 90 of 100. The second passes 90 out of every 100 that reach it, so nine tenths of 90, which is 81. Choosing 80 takes away ten twice instead of taking a tenth of what remained.

items.p: A tinted film lets through one third of the light that falls on it. What fraction of the light gets through two layers of the film? Write it as a fraction.
items.why: After one layer a third is left. The second layer lets through a third of that third, which is one third times one third, or one ninth.

items.p: A glass marble is easy to see in air but nearly vanishes in honey. A clear fish is hard to see in water. Explain both, using the words edge and bend.
items.a: We see a clear thing only where light bends or bounces at its edge. The marble in air has a big bend at its edge, so it shows. In honey there is almost no bend, so it nearly vanishes. A clear fish in water is made mostly of water, so there is almost no bend at her edge, and she is hard to see.
items.why: A strong answer says that we see edges, that the size of the bend depends on how different the two materials are, and that a fish is mostly water.

items.p: Which liquid would hide a glass marble best? Glass has a refractive index of about 1.5.
opts: A liquid with a refractive index of about 1.5
A liquid with a refractive index of about 1.33
A liquid with a refractive index of about 1
A liquid with a refractive index of about 2.4
items.why: A clear thing vanishes best when the liquid bends light by the same amount as the thing. Glass is about 1.5, so a liquid of 1.5 is the best match. Water at 1.33 is only a partial match, and 2.4 would bend light the other way and the marble would reappear.

items.p: True or false: a green glass marble could vanish completely in a perfectly matching liquid.
items.why: False. A matching liquid would hide the edge, but the green glass would still soak up some colours of light. You would see a green patch where the marble is. Only a perfectly clear marble can vanish completely.

items.p: A ruby is red but pure aluminium oxide is clear. What does the chromium do?
opts: It adds a jump of just the right size for electrons to soak up some colours of light
items.why: Chromium atoms in the crystal give electrons a jump that matches the energy of some colours of light, which are soaked up. The colours that pass on look red. The chromium is not paint, and it is only a trace.

items.p: Is each of these mostly caused by scattering, by soaking up or by bouncing back?
items: snow looks white
Scattering
a black cloth gets hot in the Sun
Soaking up
a mirror shows your face
Bouncing back
milk looks white
Scattering
dark sunglasses make a bright day softer
Soaking up
a still pond shows the evening sky
Bouncing back
items.why: Scattering sends light in all directions and makes things look white. Soaking up takes the light's energy and warms the material. Bouncing back in one tidy direction makes a picture.

items.p: Put the steps of the Two Gates test in order, from first to last.
items: Check that the lenses are polarising by looking at a bright screen through one and turning it
Look at a bright window through one lens
Hold two lenses together, lined up, and score the brightness
Turn one lens a quarter turn and score the brightness
Say what you thought, what you saw and why
items.why: First check that your lenses are polarising. Then look through one, then two lined up, then two crossed. At the end, compare what you saw with what you guessed.

items.p: A school wants to put tinted windows on its bus.

views.says: Clear windows, please. I want to be able to see my child on the bus, and to know she is safe.
Tinted windows keep out the glare and heat. The children arrive less tired.
I want to see the road and the shops outside, so I need to see out through a clear window.

items.ask: Which view do you think matters most? Give a reason, and say what kind of glass could meet more than one need.
items.a: A strong answer weighs safety, comfort and the view, and might suggest a light tint that blocks ultraviolet and cuts glare, but is still clear enough to see through. There is no single right answer, but the reason matters.
items.why: A light tint soaks up a share of the light and passes on the rest, so it can cut heat and glare while still letting people see in and out. A heavy tint trades the view for comfort.

items.p: A student says that something which is opaque to light must be opaque to every kind of wave. Which fact shows that she is wrong?
opts: X-rays go through a hand that stops sunlight
items.why: X-rays pass through skin and muscle, which stop visible light. Radio waves go through walls too. Whether a material is opaque depends on the kind of wave.

items.p: A lump of rock salt is clear, but a spoonful of table salt is white. Explain why, and say what you could do to make the table salt look clearer.
items.a: The lump of rock salt has a few smooth surfaces, and light goes through it. The table salt is made of thousands of tiny crystals, and light bends and bounces off all of their surfaces, so it scatters in every direction and the salt looks white. A drop of oil would fill the gaps between the grains and make the patch look more see-through.
items.why: A strong answer uses scattering from many surfaces, and the idea that filling the gaps with a liquid that bends light a similar amount reduces the scattering.

items.p: Draw two polarising filters, one with upright bars and one with sideways bars, with a light wave arriving, wiggling up and down. Show where it goes through and where it stops.
items.a: A wavy line passing through the filter with upright bars, and then stopped at the filter with sideways bars, with nothing coming out of the second filter.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the up-and-down wiggle passing through the first gate and being stopped at the second, which only lets sideways wiggles pass.

items.p: The edge of a thick sheet of clear window glass looks green. What is the best reason?
opts: A trace of iron in the glass soaks up some of the red light, and the thick edge soaks up enough to show
items.why: Glass contains a trace of iron. In a thin sheet it hardly shows. Looking along the edge, the light passes through a long path of glass, and more of the red is soaked up, so the green shows.

items.p: Match each sight to the reason for it.
pairs: a snowman looks white although ice is clear
light scatters off the many tiny ice crystals
a marble vanishes in honey
honey and glass bend light almost the same, so there is no bend at the edge
a hospital picture shows the bones in a hand
X-rays pass through soft parts and are stopped by bone
a red fish looks black deep in the sea
the water has soaked up the red light
items.why: All four are the same four fates of light: scatter, pass on, stop and soak up. The reason depends on what the light meets and what kind of light it is.

items.p: True or false: a material that stops visible light must also stop radio waves.
items.why: False. A brick wall stops light but lets through many radio waves, such as Wi-Fi and mobile signals, though they get weaker.

items.p: A student puts a glass marble in a liquid with a refractive index of 2.4, which is much bigger than glass. What happens to how easy the marble is to see?
opts: It is easy to see again, because the bend at the edge is big, the other way
items.why: A clear thing vanishes only when the liquid matches. If the liquid bends light much more than glass, there is a big bend at the edge again, so the marble stands out. Matching means equal, not just bigger.

quiz.p: A sheet of paper passes on 50 parts of every 100 parts of light, bounces back 30 and soaks up 10. How many parts does it scatter?
quiz.why: The four shares add up to 100. 50 plus 30 plus 10 is 90. 100 take away 90 is 10. So 10 parts are scattered, if the sheet only passes, bounces, soaks and scatters.

quiz.p: Three identical lenses are in a row, and each lets through half the light that reaches it. What fraction of the light passes through all three?
quiz.why: Half of a half is a quarter, and half of a quarter is an eighth. Each lens takes the same share of what reaches it.

quiz.p: A heat-proof glass rod nearly vanishes in a jar of cooking oil. What is the best reason?
opts: The oil bends light almost the same as the glass, so there is hardly any bend at the rod's edge
The oil is warmer than the rod
The oil is thicker than the rod
The oil soaks up the glass
quiz.why: We see a clear thing by the bend of light at its edge. When the liquid bends light by about the same amount, there is almost no bend left to see.

quiz.p: Why does a heap of clear salt crystals look white?
opts: Light scatters off the many tiny surfaces in every direction
Salt soaks up all colours except white
The crystals make their own white light
quiz.why: Each crystal is clear, but light bends and bounces at every surface, and comes back out in all directions. Mixed light from every direction looks white.

quiz.p: Why does ordinary window glass pass visible light but block most ultraviolet B?
opts: Ultraviolet photons carry enough energy to move electrons in the glass, and visible photons do not
Ultraviolet is a colour that glass reflects
quiz.why: Light comes in packets of energy, and ultraviolet packets carry more energy than visible ones. Only the larger packets can lift the electrons in glass, so the glass soaks up the ultraviolet.

quiz.p: Two polarising lenses are turned a quarter turn from each other, and no light gets through. What is the best explanation?
opts: The first lens passes only one wiggle direction, and the second blocks that direction
Each lens soaks up half of the light
The lenses reflect all the light
quiz.why: A polarising lens passes only light wiggling in one direction. A second lens turned across the first passes only the other direction, and nothing is left for it to pass.

quiz.p: You look at a laptop screen through a polarising sunglass lens, and turn the lens. The screen goes dark at one angle. What does this show?
opts: The screen's light wiggles in one direction
The lens soaks up the screen
quiz.why: A polarising lens blocks light that wiggles across it. If the screen goes dark at one angle, the light from the screen must wiggle in only one direction.

quiz.p: Which of these passes through a hand that stops sunlight?
quiz.why: X-rays pass through skin and muscle, and are stopped by bone. This shows that being opaque is about the kind of wave, not only the material.

quiz.p: Why does a red fish look black in the deep sea, where only blue light is left?
opts: She soaks up the blue light, and has no red light to send back
quiz.why: A red thing sends back red light and soaks up other colours. If no red light reaches her, she has nothing to send back, and she looks dark.

quiz.p: Why does almost every see-through animal still have dark eyes?
opts: An eye must take in some light in order to sense it
All animals must be dark somewhere
quiz.why: An eye senses light by soaking some of it up. If every bit passed straight through, there would be nothing to sense. So seeing and being completely clear cannot go together.

quiz.p: In 1895 Röntgen found rays that passed through black cardboard. What idea did this show was wrong?
opts: That anything that stops light stops every kind of ray
That light travels in straight lines
quiz.why: Many scientists thought that a thick black cover stops all rays. X-rays passed through it, so opaque only describes what a material does with one kind of wave.

quiz.p: In the Vanishing Glass test, you scored how easy the marble was to see in four places. Which result best fits the idea that we see clear things by what they do to light?
opts: The marble was easiest to see in air and hardest in honey
The marble was easiest to see in honey
The marble looked the same everywhere
quiz.why: Air bends light very differently from glass, so the marble's edge shows clearly. Honey bends light almost like glass, so the edge nearly disappears.

applications: Sunglasses and spectacles with an ultraviolet filter protect the eyes, however dark or clear the lenses look.
Hospitals use X-rays to take pictures of bones and teeth through the skin.
Wi-Fi and mobile phone signals pass through walls, so one router can serve several rooms.
Polarising sunglasses and camera filters cut the glare from water, wet roads and glass.
Laptop, phone and calculator screens use polarising filters inside to make their pictures.
Photochromic spectacle lenses, switchable privacy glass and dimmable aeroplane windows change how much light they pass on.
Microscope makers put a drop of special oil between the lens and the slide to match refractive indexes and get a sharper picture.
Engineers put clear plastic or glass parts between polarising filters to see the stress patterns inside, as bands of colour.
White paint, paper and sugar get their whiteness from many tiny surfaces that scatter light.
Detectors deep underground catch a few neutrinos from the Sun and from exploding stars, to study what happens inside them.
