open_questions.q: Why are almost all see-through animals found in water, and almost none on land?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists think that in air, the difference between a body and the air around it is so large that light would still bend and bounce at the surface. In water, the difference is small. They are still working out the whole story, and why some land animals, such as glass frogs, are partly clear.

open_questions.q: Can we make a window that is clear when we want and fully opaque or cool when we want, using almost no power?
open_questions.why_open: Switchable and dimmable glass exists, but it often costs a lot, uses power or fades with time. Engineers are working on cheaper, longer-lasting kinds.

open_questions.q: Can we make a surface that reflects no light at all, whatever the angle or colour?
open_questions.why_open: Coatings and tiny patterns on the surface, some copied from moths' eyes, cut reflection down to a tiny share. A surface that reflects nothing at every angle and every colour has not been made yet.

open_questions.q: How do animals that see polarised light use it, and what does it look like to them?
open_questions.why_open: We know that bees, ants and beetles use polarised light as a compass, and that some sea animals can tell its direction. Nobody knows what it is like to see it. Our eyes cannot tell.

open_questions.q: What can neutrinos tell us about places we cannot look at, such as the inside of the Sun or of the Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Neutrinos pass almost everything, so they carry news from deep inside. Detectors catch only a very few, so it takes years to learn from them, and scientists are building bigger ones.

open_questions.q: Could we ever make a large see-through material that is as strong as steel?
open_questions.why_open: Some clear ceramics and a few types of glass are very strong, but they are small or very expensive. Scientists do not yet know whether a large, cheap, strong, clear material is possible.

maths.problem: A clean window passes on nine tenths of the light that reaches it. 1,000 parts of light fall on the first of three identical windows in a row. How many parts get through all three?
maths.explain: Nine tenths of 1,000 is 900. Nine tenths of 900 is 810. Nine tenths of 810 is 729. So 729 parts get through all three windows.
maths.context: You learned that each layer of a see-through material passes on the same share of the light that reaches it.
maths.why_maths: Taking a share of a share, step by step, shows how light fades layer after layer, and why thick glass looks dark.

maths.problem: Four identical sunglass lenses are held in a row. Each one lets through half of the light that reaches it. 800 parts of light fall on the first lens. How many parts get through the fourth?
maths.explain: Half of 800 is 400. Half of 400 is 200. Half of 200 is 100. Half of 100 is 50. So 50 parts get through all four, which is one sixteenth of 800.
maths.context: You learned that light fades in steps, a half, a quarter, an eighth, as it goes through more layers.
maths.why_maths: Halving again and again shows the pattern in which light fades, and lets you predict how many layers will hide a lamp.

maths.problem: Made-up numbers: every 10 metres of sea water takes away half of the red light. At the surface there are 640 parts of red light. How many parts are left at 30 metres? At what depth are there fewer than 10 parts left?
maths.answer: 80 parts at 30 metres. Fewer than 10 parts are left at 70 metres.
maths.explain: At 10 metres there are 320 parts, at 20 metres 160, and at 30 metres 80. Then 40 at 40 metres, 20 at 50 metres, 10 at 60 metres and 5 at 70 metres. At 70 metres there are fewer than 10.
maths.context: You learned that sea water soaks up red light first, so red animals look black in the deep.
maths.why_maths: A halving pattern lets you predict the depth at which a colour is gone, without having to go there.

maths.problem: A clean window bounces back about 8 parts in every 100 parts of light and soaks up about 2 parts. How many parts pass on? What fraction of the light is that?
maths.explain: The four shares add up to 100. 8 plus 2 is 10. 100 take away 10 is 90, if nothing is scattered. 90 out of 100 is the same as 9 out of 10, which is nine tenths.
maths.context: You learned that the shares of light that bounce, soak, scatter and pass on add up to all of it.
maths.why_maths: Subtracting the known shares from the whole tells you the share that is left, without having to measure it.

maths.problem: In the Vanishing Glass test, a marble scores 5 in air, 4 in water, 2 in oil and 1 in honey, out of 5. How many points lower is the score in honey than in water? How many points does the score drop between water and oil?
maths.answer: 3 points lower in honey than in water. It drops 2 points between water and oil.
maths.explain: Water scored 4 and honey scored 1. 4 take away 1 is 3. Water scored 4 and oil scored 2. 4 take away 2 is 2.
maths.context: In the Vanishing Glass test, you score how easy it is to see a clear marble in air, water, oil and honey.
maths.why_maths: Comparing scores shows which liquid hides the marble best, and by how much.

maths.problem: You look at a laptop screen through a polarising lens and turn the lens through one full turn of 360 degrees. The screen is brightest when you start, at 0 degrees. It goes dark when the lens has turned a quarter turn. How many times does the screen go dark in one full turn, and at which angles?
maths.answer: Twice, at 90 degrees and at 270 degrees.
maths.explain: The screen is dark after a quarter turn, which is 90 degrees. It is bright again after a half turn, 180 degrees. After three quarters of a turn, 270 degrees, it is dark again. At 360 degrees it is bright, where you started. So it goes dark twice.
maths.context: In Two Gates for Light, you turn a polarising lens in front of a screen and watch it go dark.
maths.why_maths: Counting quarter turns shows a pattern that repeats every half turn, which matches the way a polarising filter works.

maths.problem: About 60 billion neutrinos from the Sun pass through every square centimetre each second. A thumbnail covers about 2 square centimetres. How many pass through a thumbnail in one second? How many in 10 seconds?
maths.answer: About 120 billion in one second, and about 1,200 billion, which is 1.2 trillion, in 10 seconds.
maths.explain: 2 times 60 billion is 120 billion. In 10 seconds, it is 10 times 120 billion, which is 1,200 billion. And 1,200 billion is the same as 1.2 trillion.
maths.context: You learned that neutrinos pass through almost everything, including your body.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying very large numbers helps you see just how many particles pass through you without stopping.

maths.problem: A cube of clear sugar candy has sides 1 centimetre long, so its surface area is 6 square centimetres. You crush it into 1,000 small cubes, each with sides 1 millimetre long, which is a tenth of a centimetre. What is the total surface of the small cubes?
maths.answer: 60 square centimetres. That is 10 times as much.
maths.explain: One small cube has faces of a tenth of a centimetre by a tenth, which is one hundredth of a square centimetre. It has 6 faces, so 6 hundredths of a square centimetre. 1,000 small cubes make 60 square centimetres. 60 divided by 6 is 10, so there is 10 times as much surface.
maths.context: In Clear Candy, White Powder, you crush clear sugar candy and watch it turn white.
maths.why_maths: Counting the surface shows that crushing makes far more surfaces for light to bend and bounce off, which is why powder looks white.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. Things to check before release: (1) The Vanishing Glass test depends on the marble and the honey. A plain soda-glass marble has a refractive index of about 1.52 and honey about 1.49 to 1.50, so it should nearly vanish, but a marble with swirls or bubbles will stay visible. The scores will vary. Heat-proof glass in cooking oil is a stronger match, but the unit does not rely on it. (2) Two Gates for Light needs polarising lenses. Many sunglasses are polarising but some are not, and some phone screens do not work for the screen test, so a laptop or tablet is better. The third-lens step is optional. (3) Clear Candy, White Powder works well with kalkandu, and coarse clear sugar crystals also work. (4) Ten Light Balls now works with two people, using 16 balls and half-share lenses. (5) The Tape Stained Glass colours depend on the tape and screen, and may be faint on some screens. (6) The sugar syrups in the challenge are made with warm water by a grown-up. A thick sugar syrup (refractive index about 1.45) will probably rank below oil and honey, and that is an honest result. Facts to verify: the neutrino count of about 60 billion per square centimetre per second; Marie Dacke's dung beetle result of 2003; Malus 1808 to 1809; the glass frog blood result of 2022; the 2016 transparent wood research; the Boeing 787 dimmable windows; the depths of the sunlit and twilight zones; Röntgen's date and details; Pliny's date; the claim that early glass dates from about 3,500 years ago and the dating of Indian glass beads; the refractive index of honey.
